docs.title: 5.2.2 Variational Autoencoders
docs.text:
A VAE has encoder \(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})\) and decoder \(p_\theta(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z})\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}} = -\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})}[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z})] + D_{\text{KL}}(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) \| p(\mathbf{z}))\tag{5.6}\]

The reparameterization trick: \(\mathbf{z} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_\phi + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_\phi \odot \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\), \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\), enables gradient flow through sampling.

Important

The ELBO structure directly parallels the training objective of quantum Boltzmann machines and quantum VAEs. Replacing the classical Gaussian latent with a quantum state produces the quantum generative models studied in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 5.3.1 Message Passing Neural Networks
docs.text:
A graph \(G=(V,E)\) with node features \(\mathbf{h}_v^{(0)}=\mathbf{x}_v\). Message passing for layer \(\ell\):

\[\begin{align*} \mathbf{m}_v^{(\ell)} &= \text{AGG}\!\left(\{\text{MSG}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{h}_v^{(\ell-1)}, \mathbf{h}_u^{(\ell-1)}, e_{uv}) : u\in\mathcal{N}(v)\}\right) \\ \mathbf{h}_v^{(\ell)} &= \text{UPDATE}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{h}_v^{(\ell-1)}, \mathbf{m}_v^{(\ell)}) \end{align*}\]

After \(L\) layers, readout: \(\mathbf{h}_G = \text{READOUT}(\{\mathbf{h}_v^{(L)}\}_{v\in V})\).

GCN (Kipf & Welling, 2017): \(\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)} = \sigma(\tilde{D}^{-1/2}\tilde{A}\tilde{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)})\), where \(\tilde{A} = A + I\) (self-loops), \(\tilde{D}\) is diagonal degree matrix.

Note

Quantum graph neural networks replace classical message passing with quantum operations on graph states. The graph structure maps to qubit connectivity, and quantum entanglement encodes graph topology. See Chapter 19.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Markov Decision Processes
docs.text:
An MDP is \((\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, R, \gamma)\):

  • States \(s\in\mathcal{S}\), Actions \(a\in\mathcal{A}\)

  • Transition \(P(s'|s,a)\), Reward \(R(s,a)\), Discount \(\gamma\in[0,1)\)

Value function: \(V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t R(s_t,a_t)|s_0=s\right]\). Bellman equation: \(V^\pi(s) = \sum_a\pi(a|s)\sum_{s'}P(s'|s,a)[R(s,a)+\gamma V^\pi(s')]\).

docs.title: 5.4.2 Policy Gradient (REINFORCE)
docs.text:
For a parameterized policy \(\pi_ heta\), the policy gradient theorem:

\[ abla_ heta J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_ heta}\!\left[ abla_ heta\log\pi_ heta(a|s)\cdot Q^{\pi_ heta}(s,a) ight] ag{5.9}\]

Algorithm: REINFORCE Algorithm

  1. For each episode: collect trajectory \( au = (s_0,a_0,r_0,…,s_T)\) using \(\pi_ heta\)

  2. Compute returns \(G_t = \sum_{k=t}^T \gamma^{k-t}r_k\)

  3. Update: \( heta \leftarrow heta + \eta\sum_t G_t abla_ heta\log\pi_ heta(a_t|s_t)\)

Tip

Quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) replaces the classical policy network with a parameterized quantum circuit \(U( oldsymbol{ heta})\). The policy gradient theorem applies directly — swap out the neural network for a PQC and use the parameter shift rule for gradients.

docs.title: 5.5.1 t-SNE and UMAP
docs.text:
t-SNE (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008) minimizes KL divergence between high-dimensional Gaussian similarities and low-dimensional Student-\(t\) similarities:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{t-SNE}} = \sum_{i\neq j} p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}}\tag{5.10}\]

UMAP uses topological data analysis (Riemannian manifold approximation) and is faster than t-SNE for large datasets.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

def rbf_kernel(X1, X2, length_scale=1.0, variance=1.0):
    """RBF kernel matrix."""
    diffs = X1[:, None, :] - X2[None, :, :]
    sq_dists = np.sum(diffs**2, axis=-1)
    return variance * np.exp(-0.5 * sq_dists / length_scale**2)

class GaussianProcessRegressor:
    def __init__(self, kernel=rbf_kernel, noise=1e-3):
        self.kernel = kernel
        self.noise = noise

    def fit(self, X_train, y_train):
        self.X_train = X_train
        self.y_train = y_train
        K = self.kernel(X_train, X_train)
        self.K_inv = np.linalg.inv(K + self.noise * np.eye(len(X_train)))
        self.alpha = self.K_inv @ y_train

    def predict(self, X_test, return_std=True):
        K_star = self.kernel(X_test, self.X_train)
        mean = K_star @ self.alpha
        if return_std:
            K_ss = self.kernel(X_test, X_test)
            cov = K_ss - K_star @ self.K_inv @ K_star.T
            return mean, np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))
        return mean

# Usage
X_train = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0]])
y_train = np.array([1.0, 0.5, 0.0])
gp = GaussianProcessRegressor()
gp.fit(X_train, y_train)
X_test = np.linspace(-0.5, 2.5, 50).reshape(-1, 1)
mu, sigma = gp.predict(X_test)
print(f"Prediction at x=1.5: {gp.predict(np.array([[1.5]]))[0][0]:.3f}")

docs.title: 5.6 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • Gaussian Processes: Bayesian non-parametric regression via kernel matrices. GP prediction requires \(O(N^3)\) – quantum speedup via quantum kernels.

  • Variational inference: ELBO framework for approximate Bayesian inference. Foundation for VAEs and quantum Boltzmann machines.

  • GNNs: Message passing over graph topology – quantum analogue uses quantum entanglement to encode graph structure.

  • Reinforcement learning: Policy gradient theorem applies to quantum policies via parameter shift rule.

  • Dimensionality reduction: t-SNE/UMAP as classical baselines for comparing against quantum circuit-based dimensionality reduction.

Exercises

Exercise . Derive the GP posterior mean and variance in equations (5.3) and (5.4) from the joint Gaussian conditioning formula.

Exercise . Show that maximizing the ELBO is equivalent to minimizing \(D_{\text{KL}}(q_\phi(\mathbf{z})\|p(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}))\).

Exercise . For the GCN update rule, show that when \(A\) is the adjacency matrix of a complete graph (\(K_n\)), the layer reduces to a global averaging plus self-loop term.

Exercise . Implement a 2-layer GCN using NumPy (no frameworks) for node classification on the Karate Club graph. Report accuracy.

Further Reading

  • Rasmussen & Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning (Rasmussen and Williams 2006) (free online)

  • Kipf & Welling (2017), Semi-supervised classification with GCNs (Kipf and Welling 2017)

  • Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (Sutton and Barto 2018)

docs.title: Chapter 6: Variational Quantum Circuits
docs.text:
Variational quantum circuits are the workhorse of NISQ-era quantum machine learning. A parameterized quantum circuit is trained by a classical optimizer to minimize a cost function evaluated on a quantum processor. This hybrid classical-quantum paradigm sidesteps the requirement for fault-tolerant hardware and is the basis of VQE, QAOA, variational classifiers, and most of the QML algorithms in this book.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Design and analyze parameterized quantum circuits (ansätze)

  • Quantify expressibility and entanglement capability of a PQC

  • Implement the hybrid classical-quantum training loop

  • Apply VQE to molecular energy estimation

  • Apply QAOA to combinatorial optimization problems

  • Build a variational quantum classifier in PennyLane

docs.title: 6.1.1 The Variational Principle
docs.text:
A parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) or variational quantum circuit (VQC) is a unitary \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) depending on tunable real parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^p\):

\[U(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \prod_{l=1}^L U_l(\theta_l) W_l\tag{6.1}\]

where \(W_l\) are fixed unitaries (entangling gates) and \(U_l(\theta_l) = e^{-i\theta_l G_l / 2}\) are parameterized rotations driven by Hermitian generators \(G_l\) (e.g., Pauli operators).

The quantum cost function:

\[\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \langle \psi(\boldsymbol{\theta}) | \hat{O} | \psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle = \text{Tr}[\hat{O}\, U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rho_0\, U^\dagger(\boldsymbol{\theta})]\tag{6.2}\]

where \(\rho_0 = |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes n}\) is the initial state and \(\hat{O}\) is an observable.

docs.title: 6.1.2 Ansatz Design Philosophy
docs.text:
A good ansatz balances three competing requirements:

  1. Expressibility: Can represent the target state

  2. Trainability: Gradients are non-vanishing (no barren plateau)

  3. Hardware efficiency: Shallow depth, native gate set

docs.title: 6.2.1 Hardware-Efficient Ansatz
docs.text:
Uses the native gate set of the quantum device:

Each layer: single-qubit rotations on all qubits, then a ring of CNOT gates. Repeated \(L\) times: total \(O(nL)\) parameters.

Pros: Shallow depth, hardware-native. Cons: High expressibility \(\Rightarrow\) barren plateaus for large \(n,L\).

docs.title: 6.2.2 Strongly Entangling Layers
docs.text: PennyLane’s StronglyEntanglingLayers: 3 rotations (\(R_z\), \(R_y\), \(R_z\)) per qubit, then CNOT gates with skip-\(s\) connectivity.

docs.title: 6.2.3 Data Re-uploading Ansatz
docs.text:
Introduced by Pérez-Salinas et al. (2020) (Pérez-Salinas et al. 2020): encode classical data multiple times in the circuit, interleaved with trainable rotations:

\[U(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \prod_{l=1}^L S(\mathbf{x})W(\boldsymbol{\theta}_l)\tag{6.3}\]

where \(S(\mathbf{x})\) is the data encoding and \(W(\boldsymbol{\theta}_l)\) is a trainable layer. This is a universal quantum classifier for \(r\) sufficiently large.

docs.title: 6.3 Expressibility and Entanglement Capability
docs.text:
Expressibility (Sim et al. 2019): measures how well a PQC approximates the Haar random distribution over unitaries. Formally:

\[\mathcal{A}_{\text{expr}} = D_{\text{KL}}\!\left(\hat{P}_{U(\boldsymbol{\theta})} \| P_{\text{Haar}}\right)\tag{6.4}\]

Smaller \(\mathcal{A}_{\text{expr}}\) \(\Rightarrow\) more expressive (but more barren-plateau prone).

Entanglement capability: Meyer-Wallach measure over sampled parameter vectors:

\[Q = \frac{2}{p}\sum_k\left(1 - \text{Tr}[\rho_k^2]\right), \quad \rho_k = \text{Tr}_{\neq k}[|\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle\langle\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})|]\tag{6.5}\]

docs.title: 6.4 The Hybrid Classical-Quantum Loop
docs.text:
Figure 6.1. The hybrid classical-quantum training loop. Classical optimizer proposes \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\); quantum processor evaluates \(\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\); gradient is computed via parameter shift rule; optimizer updates \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). Figure drawn for this book

The parameter shift rule (Mitarai et al. 2018; Schuld et al. 2019) computes exact quantum gradients:

\[\frac{\partial\mathcal{C}}{\partial\theta_i} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\theta}+\frac{\pi}{2}\mathbf{e}_i) - \mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\frac{\pi}{2}\mathbf{e}_i)\right]\tag{6.6}\]

This requires 2 circuit evaluations per parameter (vs. \(O(p^2)\) for finite differences). See Chapter 15 for the full derivation.

docs.title: 6.5 Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE)
docs.text:
Problem: Estimate ground state energy \(E_0 = \min_{|\psi\rangle}\langle\psi|\hat{H}|\psi\rangle\). Variational principle: \(E_0 \leq \langle\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})|\hat{H}|\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle\) for any \(|\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle\).

Algorithm: Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE)

Input: Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}=\sum_k c_k P_k\) (Pauli decomposition), ansatz \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\). Output: Approximation to ground state energy \(\tilde{E}_0\).

  1. Initialize \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(0)}\) randomly

  2. Repeat until convergence:

    1. For each Pauli term \(P_k\): evaluate \(\langle P_k\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) on QPU (shot-based)

    2. Compute cost: \(\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_k c_k \langle P_k\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\)

    3. Compute gradient via parameter shift rule

    4. Update: \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \eta\nabla\mathcal{C}\)

  3. Return \(\tilde{E}_0 = \mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^*)\)

Solved Example 6.1

Problem: Apply 1-qubit VQE to \(\hat{H} = Z\) with ansatz \(R_y(\theta)|0\rangle\).

Solution: \(|\psi(\theta)\rangle = \cos(\theta/2)|0\rangle + \sin(\theta/2)|1\rangle\). \(\mathcal{C}(\theta) = \langle\psi|Z|\psi\rangle = \cos^2(\theta/2) - \sin^2(\theta/2) = \cos\theta\). Minimum at \(\theta^* = \pi\): \(\mathcal{C}(\pi) = -1 = E_0\) (ground state \(|1\rangle\)).

docs.title: 6.6 Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)
docs.text:
Problem class: Combinatorial optimization \(\min_{\mathbf{z}\in\{-1,+1\}^n} C(\mathbf{z})\). Express as Ising Hamiltonian: \(H_C = \sum_{(i,j)\in E} w_{ij}Z_iZ_j\).

QAOA circuit (\(p\) layers):

\[|\boldsymbol{\gamma},\boldsymbol{\beta}\rangle = e^{-i\beta_p H_B} e^{-i\gamma_p H_C} \cdots e^{-i\beta_1 H_B} e^{-i\gamma_1 H_C} |+\rangle^{\otimes n}\tag{6.7}\]

where \(H_B = \sum_i X_i\) (mixer) and \(H_C\) encodes the objective.

Cost function: \(F_p(\boldsymbol{\gamma},\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \langle\boldsymbol{\gamma},\boldsymbol{\beta}|H_C|\boldsymbol{\gamma},\boldsymbol{\beta}\rangle\).

Figure 6.2. QAOA for MaxCut. Left: input graph with cut edges shown dashed. Right: \(p=1\) QAOA landscape — optimization finds optimal \((\gamma^*,\beta^*)\). Figure drawn for this book

Solved Example 6.2

Problem: Set up QAOA \(p=1\) for MaxCut on the 3-node triangle graph \(G = (\{0,1,2\}, \{(0,1),(1,2),(0,2)\})\).

Solution: MaxCut objective: \(C(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j)\in E}(1-z_iz_j)\). Ising Hamiltonian: \(H_C = -\frac{1}{2}(Z_0Z_1 + Z_1Z_2 + Z_0Z_2) + \frac{3}{2}I\). Mixer: \(H_B = X_0 + X_1 + X_2\). Initial state: \(|{+}{+}{+}\rangle\). Circuit: apply \(e^{-i\gamma H_C}\) (3 ZZ rotations) then \(e^{-i\beta H_B}\) (3 Rx rotations). Optimize \(F_1(\gamma,\beta) = \langle H_C\rangle\) over \((\gamma,\beta)\). For this graph, MaxCut = 2 (achievable by many partitions).

docs.title: 6.7 Variational Quantum Classifier
docs.text:
Architecture: data encoding \(U_\phi(\mathbf{x})\) followed by trainable ansatz \(W(\boldsymbol{\theta})\).

\[|\psi(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle = W(\boldsymbol{\theta})\, U_\phi(\mathbf{x})\, |0\rangle^{\otimes n}\tag{6.8}\]

Output: \(\hat{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \text{sign}(\langle Z_0\rangle_{\psi(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\theta})})\). Loss: cross-entropy or hinge loss on \(\{\langle Z_0\rangle\}_{i=1}^N\).

import pennylane as qml
import numpy as np
from pennylane import numpy as pnp

n_qubits = 4
dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits)

# -- VQE for Hydrogen ------------------------------------------
H2_coeffs = [-0.2252, 0.1777, 0.1777, -0.2427, -0.2427, 0.1706, 0.1706]
H2_ops = [qml.Identity(0), qml.PauliZ(0), qml.PauliZ(1),
           qml.PauliZ(0)@qml.PauliZ(1), qml.PauliY(0)@qml.PauliY(1),
           qml.PauliX(0)@qml.PauliX(1), qml.PauliZ(2)]
H2 = qml.Hamiltonian(H2_coeffs[:4], H2_ops[:4])  # simplified

dev_vqe = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=2)

@qml.qnode(dev_vqe)
def vqe_circuit(params):
    qml.RY(params[0], wires=0)
    qml.RY(params[1], wires=1)
    qml.CNOT(wires=[0, 1])
    qml.RY(params[2], wires=0)
    return qml.expval(H2)

opt = qml.GradientDescentOptimizer(stepsize=0.4)
params = pnp.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3], requires_grad=True)
for step in range(100):
    params, energy = opt.step_and_cost(vqe_circuit, params)
    if step
        print(f"Step {step:3d} | Energy = {energy:.6f} Ha")

# -- QAOA for MaxCut -------------------------------------------
dev_qaoa = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=4)
edges = [(0,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,0)]  # 4-node ring

def qaoa_layer(gamma, beta):
    for i, j in edges:
        qml.IsingZZ(2 * gamma, wires=[i, j])
    for i in range(4):
        qml.RX(2 * beta, wires=i)

@qml.qnode(dev_qaoa)
def qaoa_circuit(params, n_layers=2):
    for i in range(4): qml.Hadamard(i)
    for l in range(n_layers):
        qaoa_layer(params[2*l], params[2*l+1])
    return qml.expval(qml.sum(*[qml.PauliZ(i)@qml.PauliZ(j) for i,j in edges]))

params = pnp.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.8, 0.2], requires_grad=True)
opt_qaoa = qml.AdamOptimizer(stepsize=0.1)
for step in range(50):
    params, cost = opt_qaoa.step_and_cost(qaoa_circuit, params)
print(f"QAOA MaxCut cost: {-cost:.4f}")

docs.title: 6.8 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • PQC: Parameterized quantum circuit \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) as a trainable model. Output is expectation value \(\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\langle\hat{O}\rangle\).

  • Ansatz architectures: Hardware-efficient, strongly entangling, UCCSD (chemistry), data re-uploading. Each trades expressibility vs. trainability.

  • Expressibility: Closeness of PQC ensemble to Haar measure. High expressibility \(\Rightarrow\) barren plateaus.

  • Hybrid loop: Classical optimizer + quantum cost evaluation. Gradients via parameter shift rule (2 circuit evaluations per parameter).

  • VQE: Minimize \(\langle\hat{H}\rangle\) to approximate ground state energy. Used for quantum chemistry and materials science.

  • QAOA: \(p\)-layer alternating problem/mixer Hamiltonians for combinatorial optimization. Exact at \(p\to\infty\).

  • VQC: Data encoding + trainable ansatz = parameterized classifier. Training uses cross-entropy loss + parameter shift gradients.

Exercises

Exercise . For a 2-qubit hardware-efficient ansatz with 1 layer, how many parameters does it have? Write out the full circuit unitary as a product of matrices.

Exercise . Verify the parameter shift rule for \(\mathcal{C}(\theta) = \langle 0|R_y^\dagger(\theta) Z R_y(\theta)|0\rangle\). Compute the gradient analytically and confirm it equals \(\frac{1}{2}[\mathcal{C}(\theta+\pi/2)-\mathcal{C}(\theta-\pi/2)]\).

Exercise . For the 1-qubit VQE with \(\hat{H} = aX + bZ\), find the optimal angle \(\theta^*\) that minimizes the energy. What is \(E_0\)?

Exercise . Show that for \(p\to\infty\), QAOA can exactly solve any optimization problem. Hint: Show that QAOA can represent adiabatic evolution.

Exercise . Implement a VQC for binary classification on the make_moons dataset using PennyLane with 2 qubits, angle encoding, and 2 strongly entangling layers. Compare accuracy to a classical SVM with RBF kernel.

Further Reading

  • Peruzzo et al. (2014) (Peruzzo et al. 2014) — original VQE paper

  • Farhi et al. (2014) (Farhi et al. 2014) — original QAOA paper

  • Schuld et al. (2020) (Schuld et al. 2021) — circuit-centric quantum classifier

  • Sim et al. (2019) (Sim et al. 2019) — expressibility and entanglement capability

docs.title: Chapter 7: Quantum Feature Maps and Data Encoding
docs.text:
How do we get classical data into a quantum computer? This question — the data encoding problem — is among the most practically important in QML. The choice of encoding determines the inductive bias, computational overhead, and potential quantum advantage of any QML model. This chapter surveys the major encoding strategies and their theoretical properties.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Implement amplitude, angle, basis, and IQP-style encodings

  • Analyze the expressibility and inductive bias of each encoding

  • Explain the data re-uploading approach and its universality

  • Discuss the qRAM assumption and its practical challenges

  • Design custom feature maps for specific data types

docs.title: 7.1 The Data Encoding Problem
docs.text:
Classical data \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) must be mapped to a quantum state \(|\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^{2^n}\). The mapping is a quantum feature map:

\[\mathbf{x} \mapsto |\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle = U_\phi(\mathbf{x})|0\rangle^{\otimes n}\tag{7.1}\]

The induced quantum kernel is the fidelity:

\[k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = |\langle\phi(\mathbf{x})|\phi(\mathbf{x}')\rangle|^2 = |\langle 0|U_\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{x}')U_\phi(\mathbf{x})|0\rangle|^2\tag{7.2}\]

Warning

Every encoding strategy makes implicit choices about which data similarities are preserved. A mismatch between the encoding’s inductive bias and the true data geometry can lead to poor generalization — regardless of quantum hardware quality.

docs.title: 7.2 Amplitude Encoding
docs.text:
Definition: Amplitude Encoding

Given \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{2^n}\) with \(\|\mathbf{x}\|=1\), amplitude encoding maps:

\[\mathbf{x} = [x_0, x_1, …, x_{2^n-1}]^\top \mapsto |\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle = \sum_{i=0}^{2^n-1} x_i |i\rangle\tag{7.3}\]

Requires \(n = \lceil\log_2 d\rceil\) qubits to encode \(d\) features.

Pros: Exponential compression (\(2^n\) features in \(n\) qubits).

Cons: State preparation requires \(O(2^n)\) gates in general; needs qRAM.

Induced kernel: \(k_Q^{\text{amp}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = |\langle\phi(\mathbf{x})|\phi(\mathbf{x}')\rangle|^2 = (\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}')^2\) for real vectors.

Important

The qRAM assumption: Loading \(N\) classical data points via amplitude encoding requires a quantum random access memory (qRAM) device, which can prepare arbitrary superpositions in \(O(\text{poly}(\log N))\) time. No qRAM at scale exists in 2025. This critically limits amplitude encoding in practice.

docs.title: 7.3 Angle Encoding
docs.text:
Definition: Angle Encoding

Each feature \(x_i\) is encoded as a rotation angle on qubit \(i\):

\[U_\phi(\mathbf{x}) = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n R_y(x_i) = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n \begin{pmatrix}\cos(x_i/2) & -\sin(x_i/2) \\ \sin(x_i/2) & \cos(x_i/2)\end{pmatrix}\tag{7.4}\]

Result: \(|\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n (\cos(x_i/2)|0\rangle + \sin(x_i/2)|1\rangle)\).

Pros: Simple, hardware-efficient, depth-1 circuit. Cons: Requires \(n = d\) qubits; product state (no entanglement initially).

Variants:

  • ZZ encoding: \(U = \prod_{i < j} R_{ZZ}(x_ix_j) \prod_i R_z(x_i)\)

  • Pauli encoding: Rotate each qubit about \(X\), \(Y\), or \(Z\) axis

  • Full encoding: \(R_z(x_i)R_y(x_{i+n})R_z(x_{i+2n})\) using 3 angles per qubit

docs.title: 7.4 IQP-Style Feature Maps
docs.text:
Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial (IQP) circuits consist of diagonal gates (in the computational basis) sandwiched between Hadamard layers:

\[U_{\text{IQP}}(\mathbf{x}) = H^{\otimes n} \exp\!\left(i\sum_{S\subseteq[n]} x_S \prod_{j\in S} Z_j\right) H^{\otimes n}\tag{7.5}\]

Quantum advantage claim (Liu et al. 2021): For certain IQP-based kernels, classical simulation requires exponential time (unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses). This provides a provable separation between quantum and classical kernels for specific learning tasks.

docs.title: 7.5 Data Re-Uploading
docs.text:
Introduced by Pérez-Salinas et al. (2020) (Pérez-Salinas et al. 2020): encode data \(r\) times, interleaved with trainable rotations.

Universality theorem: A single-qubit circuit with \(r \geq 2n+1\) re-uploads can approximate any continuous function of \(n\) inputs to arbitrary accuracy.

Solved Example 7.1

Problem: Design a 1-qubit data re-uploading circuit for \(f(x) = \sin(2x)\cos(x)\) using \(r=3\) uploads of \(x\).

Solution: Circuit: \(U = R_z(\theta_3)R_y(x)R_z(\theta_2)R_y(x)R_z(\theta_1)R_y(x)\). The Fourier series generated by 3 uploads of \(x\) contains frequencies \(\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}\) — sufficient to represent \(f(x) = \sin(2x)\cos(x) = \frac{1}{2}(\sin(3x)+\sin(x))\). Train \(\{\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3\}\) to minimize \(\ell = \sum_k(\langle Z\rangle_k - f(x_k))^2\).

docs.title: 7.6 Basis Encoding and Computational Basis
docs.text:
For binary/integer data \(\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^n\):

\[|\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle = |x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n\rangle\]

Pros: Trivial state preparation (\(O(n)\) \(X\) gates). Cons: Only handles discrete data; no smoothness in the kernel.

docs.title: 7.7 Comparison of Encoding Strategies
7.8 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • Amplitude encoding: \(n = \log_2 d\) qubits but requires \(O(d)\)-depth state preparation or qRAM. Induced kernel = dot-product squared.

  • Angle encoding: One qubit per feature, depth-1. Simple and practical. Product kernel structure; no entanglement before ansatz.

  • IQP encoding: Creates non-trivial quantum correlations via ZZ interactions. Provably hard to simulate classically, enabling quantum kernel advantage.

  • Data re-uploading: Universal quantum classifier with a single-qubit. Generates Fourier series in the data; expressibility grows with repeats.

  • Choice matters: Encoding determines inductive bias. Matching the encoding to data structure is as important as the ansatz.

Exercises

Exercise . For angle encoding \(|\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle = \bigotimes_i (\cos(x_i/2)|0\rangle + \sin(x_i/2)|1\rangle)\), compute the quantum kernel \(k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = |\langle\phi(\mathbf{x})|\phi(\mathbf{x}')\rangle|^2\). Show it factors as \(\prod_i \cos^2\!\big(\frac{x_i-x_i'}{2}\big)\).

Exercise . Design a 3-qubit amplitude encoding circuit for \(\mathbf{x} = [1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 0, 0, 0, 0]^\top/\sqrt{2}\). Write the gate sequence.

Exercise . Prove that data re-uploading with \(r\) uploads of \(d\)-dimensional data on \(n\) qubits can generate Fourier coefficients with frequencies up to \(r\) in each dimension.

Exercise . Compute and visualize the kernel matrix \(\mathbf{K}_{ij} = k_Q(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)\) for both angle encoding and IQP encoding on the Iris dataset (first 2 features, 30 points). Compare the kernel matrices as heatmaps.

Further Reading

  • Schuld & Killoran (2019) (Schuld et al. 2019) — quantum feature spaces and kernels

  • Pérez-Salinas et al. (2020) (Pérez-Salinas et al. 2020) — data re-uploading

  • Liu et al. (2021) (Liu et al. 2021) — quantum kernel learning advantage

docs.title: Chapter 8: Quantum Kernel Methods
docs.text:
Quantum kernels provide one of the most theoretically grounded bridges between quantum computing and machine learning. By measuring the inner product between quantum feature states, we obtain a kernel function that can be plugged into any classical kernel method — SVM, Gaussian process, kernel PCA — while potentially capturing data similarities that are intractable to compute classically.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Define and estimate quantum kernels via the swap test and Hadamard test

  • Analyze the RKHS induced by a quantum feature map

  • Apply quantum kernel alignment to train the feature map

  • Understand projected quantum kernels and classical shadow kernels

  • Critically evaluate quantum kernel advantage claims

docs.title: 8.1 From Classical to Quantum Kernels
docs.text:
In classical kernel methods, \(k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = \langle\phi(\mathbf{x}),\phi(\mathbf{x}')\rangle_\mathcal{H}\) for some (possibly infinite-dimensional) feature map \(\phi\).

The quantum kernel analogously uses a quantum feature map \(|\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle = U_\phi(\mathbf{x})|0\rangle^{\otimes n}\):

\[k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = |\langle\phi(\mathbf{x})|\phi(\mathbf{x}')\rangle|^2 = \left|\langle 0|^{\otimes n} U_\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{x}')U_\phi(\mathbf{x})|0\rangle^{\otimes n}\right|^2\tag{8.1}\]

This is the fidelity kernel: \(k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = F(|\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle,|\phi(\mathbf{x}')\rangle)\).

Note

The quantum kernel defines a RKHS associated with the feature map \(|\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle\). The SVM classification function in this RKHS is: \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_i)\), identical to classical kernel SVM with \(k \to k_Q\).

docs.title: 8.2.1 Hadamard Test
docs.text:
The Hadamard test estimates \(\text{Re}\langle\psi|U|\psi\rangle\) using an ancilla qubit:

For computing \(k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = |\langle 0|U_\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{x}')U_\phi(\mathbf{x})|0\rangle|^2\), set \(U = U_\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{x}')U_\phi(\mathbf{x})\) and \(|\psi\rangle = |0\rangle^{\otimes n}\):

\(P(0) = \frac{1}{2}(1 + \text{Re}\langle\phi(\mathbf{x}')|\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle)\), \(k_Q = |2P(0)-1|^2\) when the kernel is real.

docs.title: 8.2.2 Direct Fidelity Estimation
docs.text:
More practical: apply \(U_\phi(\mathbf{x})\), then \(U_\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{x}')\), and measure probability of \(|0\rangle^{\otimes n}\):

\[k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = P(|0\rangle^{\otimes n}) = |\langle 0|U_\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{x}')U_\phi(\mathbf{x})|0\rangle|^2\tag{8.2}\]

This requires \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\) shots to estimate to precision \(\epsilon\).

Solved Example 8.1

Problem: Compute \(k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')\) for angle encoding with \(\mathbf{x}=[0.5]\) and \(\mathbf{x}'=[1.0]\) on 1 qubit.

Solution: \(|\phi(0.5)\rangle = \cos(0.25)|0\rangle+\sin(0.25)|1\rangle\), \(|\phi(1.0)\rangle = \cos(0.5)|0\rangle+\sin(0.5)|1\rangle\). \(\langle\phi(1.0)|\phi(0.5)\rangle = \cos(0.5)\cos(0.25)+\sin(0.5)\sin(0.25) = \cos(0.5-0.25) = \cos(0.25)\). \(k_Q = \cos^2(0.25) = 0.938\).

docs.title: 8.3 Quantum Kernel Properties
docs.text:
Figure 8.1. Comparison of kernel matrices for a two-class dataset: linear kernel (left), RBF kernel (centre), and quantum ZZ feature map kernel (right). The red lines mark the class boundary at sample 15. The quantum kernel produces a block structure with stronger intra-class similarity. Figure drawn for this book

Positive definiteness: The fidelity kernel \(k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')\) is always positive definite (it is the squared norm of a vector in a Hilbert space). Therefore it satisfies Mercer’s conditions.

Universality (Schuld 2021): A quantum kernel is universal for a domain \(\mathcal{X}\) if its associated RKHS is dense in \(C(\mathcal{X})\). IQP-based kernels can be universal for appropriate choices of feature map.

Kernel alignment:

\[\text{KTA}(\mathbf{K}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{\langle\mathbf{K}, \mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}^\top\rangle_F}{\|\mathbf{K}\|_F \|\mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}^\top\|_F}\tag{8.3}\]

Measures how well kernel matrix aligns with labels. Used as training objective for trainable quantum kernels.

docs.title: 8.4 Projected Quantum Kernels
docs.text:
Huang et al. (2021) (Huang et al. 2021) introduced projected quantum kernels that avoid the exponential concentration problem:

\[k_{\text{proj}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = \exp\!\left(-\gamma\sum_{k=1}^n \|\rho_k(\mathbf{x})-\rho_k(\mathbf{x}')\|_F^2\right)\tag{8.4}\]

where \(\rho_k(\mathbf{x}) = \text{Tr}_{\neq k}[|\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle\langle\phi(\mathbf{x})|]\) is the single-qubit reduced density matrix of qubit \(k\).

Classical shadow kernels: Compute \(\rho_k\) efficiently using classical shadows (randomized measurements), avoiding direct fidelity estimation.

docs.title: 8.5 Quantum Kernel Advantage
docs.text:
Theorem 8.1 (Quantum Kernel Advantage (Liu et al. 2021))

There exists a learning problem and a quantum kernel \(k_Q\) such that:

  1. A quantum kernel SVM achieves accuracy \(\geq 1-\epsilon\) with \(O(\text{poly}(n))\) samples

  2. Any classical kernel method requires \(\Omega(2^n)\) samples

(under standard cryptographic assumptions).

Warning

This advantage requires: (1) the problem must be constructed to favor the quantum kernel, (2) quantum hardware access with low noise, and (3) efficient kernel estimation. For naturally occurring datasets, provable quantum kernel advantage has not been demonstrated.

docs.title: 8.6 Trainable Quantum Kernels
docs.text:
Instead of a fixed feature map \(U_\phi(\mathbf{x})\), use a parameterized map \(U_\phi(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\lambda})\) and train \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) to maximize kernel-target alignment (Hubregtsen et al. 2022):

\[\boldsymbol{\lambda}^* = \operatorname{argmax}_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} \frac{\langle\mathbf{K}_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}, \mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}^\top\rangle_F}{\|\mathbf{K}_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\|_F}\tag{8.5}\]

Gradients of KTA w.r.t. \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) via parameter shift rule.

import pennylane as qml
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

n_qubits = 4
dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits)

@qml.qnode(dev)
def kernel_circuit(x1, x2):
    """Compute |<phi(x2)|phi(x1)>|^2 via overlap circuit."""
    # Encode x1
    qml.AngleEmbedding(x1[:n_qubits], wires=range(n_qubits))
    qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers(
        np.random.randn(2, n_qubits, 3), wires=range(n_qubits))
    # Adjoint of x2 encoding
    qml.adjoint(qml.AngleEmbedding)(x2[:n_qubits], wires=range(n_qubits))
    return qml.probs(wires=range(n_qubits))

def quantum_kernel(X1, X2):
    """Compute quantum kernel matrix K[i,j] = k_Q(X1[i], X2[j])."""
    n1, n2 = len(X1), len(X2)
    K = np.zeros((n1, n2))
    for i in range(n1):
        for j in range(n2):
            probs = kernel_circuit(X1[i], X2[j])
            K[i, j] = probs[0]  # P(|000...0>) = |<0|U_dag U|0>|^2
    return K

# Dataset
X, y = make_moons(n_samples=60, noise=0.15, random_state=42)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3)

# Compute kernel matrices
K_train = quantum_kernel(X_train, X_train)
K_test  = quantum_kernel(X_test, X_train)

# Train SVM with precomputed quantum kernel
svm = SVC(kernel='precomputed')
svm.fit(K_train, y_train)
accuracy = svm.score(K_test, y_test)
print(f"Quantum Kernel SVM Accuracy: {accuracy:.3f}")

# Kernel target alignment
def kernel_target_alignment(K, y):
    y_vec = 2*y - 1  # to {-1, +1}
    kta = np.dot(K.flatten(), np.outer(y_vec, y_vec).flatten())
    return kta / (np.linalg.norm(K) * np.linalg.norm(np.outer(y_vec, y_vec)))
kta = kernel_target_alignment(K_train, y_train)
print(f"Kernel-Target Alignment: {kta:.4f}")

docs.title: 8.7 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • Quantum kernel: Fidelity \(k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=|\langle\phi(\mathbf{x})|\phi(\mathbf{x}')\rangle|^2\). Always positive definite. Plugs into any classical kernel method.

  • Estimation: Direct overlap (measure \(|0\rangle\) probability after \(U_\phi U_\phi^\dagger\)) or Hadamard test. Requires \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\) shots.

  • Projected kernels: Avoid exponential concentration by using reduced density matrices of individual qubits.

  • Trainable kernels: Optimize feature map parameters via kernel alignment (KTA) to maximize separability.

  • Quantum advantage: Provable in theory (Liu 2021) for constructed problems. Not yet demonstrated on natural datasets.

Exercises

Exercise . Show that the quantum fidelity kernel \(k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = |\langle\phi(\mathbf{x})|\phi(\mathbf{x}')\rangle|^2\) is positive semi-definite.

Exercise . For angle encoding on 1 qubit, show that \(k_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = \cos^2\!\big(\frac{x-x'}{2}\big)\). Plot \(k_Q(0, x')\) for \(x'\in[-\pi,\pi]\).

Exercise . Derive the gradient of the kernel-target alignment \(\text{KTA}(\mathbf{K}_\lambda,\mathbf{y})\) with respect to a parameter \(\lambda_i\) in the feature map circuit.

Exercise . Implement the projected quantum kernel using classical shadows in PennyLane. Compare its kernel matrix to the standard fidelity kernel on a 4-qubit system.

Further Reading

  • Schuld & Killoran (2019) (Schuld et al. 2019) — quantum machine learning in feature Hilbert spaces

  • Havlíček et al. (2019) (Havlíček et al. 2019) — supervised learning with quantum enhanced feature spaces

  • Huang et al. (2021) (Huang et al. 2021) — power of data in quantum machine learning

  • Liu et al. (2021) (Liu et al. 2021) — rigorous quantum advantage for learning

docs.title: Chapter 9: Quantum Support Vector Machines
docs.text:
The quantum support vector machine (QSVM) was one of the first QML algorithms to claim an exponential speedup over classical methods. This claim has since been refined, challenged by dequantization results, and recast in the quantum kernel framework. This chapter traces the full story: the original HHL-based QSVM, the quantum kernel SVM, and an honest accounting of when — and when not — to expect quantum advantage.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Explain the HHL-based QSVM and its assumptions

  • Implement a quantum kernel SVM using PennyLane

  • Apply multi-class QSVM strategies

  • Critically evaluate QSVM vs. classical SVM benchmarks

  • Understand dequantization results and their implications for QSVM

docs.title: 9.1 The HHL-Based QSVM (Rebentrost 2014)
docs.text:
Rebentrost, Mohseni, and Lloyd (2014) (Rebentrost et al. 2014) proposed using HHL to solve the SVM kernel equation:

\[\begin{pmatrix} 0 & \mathbf{1}^\top \\ \mathbf{1} & \mathbf{K} + \gamma^{-1}I \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} b \\ \boldsymbol{\alpha} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \mathbf{y} \end{pmatrix}\tag{9.1}\]

Claimed complexity: \(O(\log(N) \kappa^2/\epsilon)\) for training (vs. \(O(N^2)\) classically).

Prediction: Quantum state \(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}\rangle\propto\sum_i\alpha_i|i\rangle\); classify new point \(|\mathbf{x}\rangle\) via inner product estimation.

Warning

Critical assumptions for HHL-QSVM speedup:

  1. qRAM for loading classical data in \(O(\log N)\) time

  2. Efficient quantum state tomography (contradicts quantum advantage)

  3. Low condition number \(\kappa = O(\text{polylog}(N))\)

  4. Only need the quantum state \(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}\rangle\), not all components

Assumption 1 requires hardware not yet available at scale. Assumption 2 is exponentially expensive. Most practical problems violate assumption 3.

docs.title: 9.2 Dequantization of QSVM
docs.text:
Tang (2019) (Tang 2019) showed that under the same \(\ell^2\)-norm sampling assumption used by HHL-QSVM:

A classical algorithm achieves the same asymptotic performance as HHL-QSVM up to polynomial factors in \(\kappa\) and \(\epsilon\).

The key insight: \(\ell^2\)-norm sampling (classical) mimics amplitude estimation (quantum). With qRAM, the quantum algorithm’s data loading advantage also provides a classical algorithm with fast sampling.

Research Highlight: Ewin Tang’s Dequantization (2019)

Ewin Tang, then an undergraduate at UT Austin, proved that quantum-inspired classical algorithms can achieve the same asymptotic runtime as the HHL-QSVM for recommendation systems (which maps to QSVM via kernel equation). This “dequantization” result was awarded the STOC 2022 Best Paper. It does not eliminate quantum advantage but forces a reassessment: quantum advantage requires problems where even \(\ell^2\)-norm sampling is difficult classically.

docs.title: 9.3 Quantum Kernel SVM (Practical Approach)
docs.text:
The practical QSVM (Havlíček et al. 2019): use a quantum device to compute \(k_Q(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)\) and solve the SVM optimization classically.

Algorithm:

Algorithm: Quantum Kernel SVM (QKSVM)

Input: Data \(\{(\mathbf{x}_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^N\), feature map \(U_\phi\), cost \(C\). Output: SVM classifier \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \text{sign}(\sum_i\alpha_iy_ik_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_i)+b)\).

  1. Kernel evaluation (quantum): compute \(K_{ij} = k_Q(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)\) for all \(i,j\) using overlap circuits. Requires \(O(N^2)\) circuit runs.

  2. SVM training (classical): solve the dual QP (4.6) with \(K_{ij}\) as the kernel matrix. Cost: \(O(N^3)\) (or \(O(N^2)\) via SMO).

  3. Prediction: \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \text{sign}\bigl(\sum_i\alpha_iy_ik_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_i)+b\bigr)\) requires \(O(N)\) kernel evaluations.

Total complexity: \(O(N^2)\) quantum + \(O(N^3)\) classical.

Solved Example 9.1

Problem: Build a QKSVM for 4-point XOR-like data: \(\mathcal{D} = \{([0,0]^\top,{+1}),([1,1]^\top,{+1}),([0,1]^\top,{-1}),([1,0]^\top,{-1})\}\).

Solution: Use angle encoding on 2 qubits: \(|\phi(\mathbf{x})\rangle = R_y(x_1)|0\rangle \otimes R_y(x_2)|0\rangle\). Compute \(K_{ij}=k_Q(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)=\cos^2\!\big(\frac{x_1^i-x_1^j}{2}\big)\cos^2\!\big(\frac{x_2^i-x_2^j}{2}\big)\).

\(K = \begin{pmatrix}1 & K_{12} & K_{13} & K_{14}\\ & 1 & K_{23} & K_{24}\\ & & 1 & K_{34}\\ & & & 1\end{pmatrix}\)

\(K_{12} = \cos^2(0)\cos^2(0)=1\), \(K_{13}=\cos^2(0)\cos^2(0.5)=0.770\), \(K_{14}=\cos^2(0.5)\cos^2(0)=0.770\), \(K_{23}=0.770\), \(K_{24}=0.770\), \(K_{34}=1\).

This kernel doesn’t separate XOR — we need an entangling feature map (e.g., IQP) to achieve non-linear separation.

docs.title: 9.4 Multi-Class Quantum SVM
docs.text:
For \(C>2\) classes, extend via:

  • One-vs-All (OvA): Train \(C\) binary classifiers \(f_c(\mathbf{x}) = k_Q\)-SVM for class \(c\) vs. rest. Predict \(\hat{y} = \operatorname{argmax}_c f_c(\mathbf{x})\).

  • One-vs-One (OvO): Train \(\binom{C}{2}\) classifiers for each pair. Predict by majority vote.

  • Direct multi-class: Measure multi-outcome observable \(\hat{O}\) with \(C\) distinct eigenvalues; each class maps to one eigenvalue.

docs.title: 9.5 Benchmarking: Fair Comparison
docs.text:
Research Highlight: Bowles et al. (2024): Fair Benchmarking

A 2024 study (Bowles et al. 2024) systematically compared quantum kernel SVMs against classical methods on 12 datasets under fair conditions (same training data, same preprocessing, same computational budget). Key findings:

  • Quantum kernels do not outperform classical RBF-SVM on any real dataset

  • Performance gap grows with dataset size (classical scales better)

  • Quantum kernels perform comparably only on tiny datasets (\(N<100\))

  • Constructed datasets (not naturally occurring) show quantum kernel advantage

Implication: Real quantum advantage for natural datasets remains elusive. Practitioners should use quantum kernels as a research tool, not a production shortcut.

import pennylane as qml
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

# IQP-style quantum kernel
n_qubits = 4
dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits)

@qml.qnode(dev)
def iqp_kernel_circuit(x1, x2):
    """IQP feature map overlap circuit."""
    def feature_map(x):
        qml.broadcast(qml.Hadamard, wires=range(n_qubits), pattern="single")
        for i in range(n_qubits):
            qml.RZ(x[i], wires=i)
        for i in range(n_qubits-1):
            qml.IsingZZ((np.pi-x[i])*(np.pi-x[i+1]), wires=[i,i+1])
        qml.broadcast(qml.Hadamard, wires=range(n_qubits), pattern="single")
    feature_map(x1)
    qml.adjoint(feature_map)(x2)
    return qml.probs(wires=range(n_qubits))

def qsvm_kernel_matrix(X1, X2):
    """Full N1 x N2 quantum kernel matrix."""
    K = np.zeros((len(X1), len(X2)))
    for i, x1 in enumerate(X1):
        for j, x2 in enumerate(X2):
            K[i, j] = iqp_kernel_circuit(x1, x2)[0]
    return K

# Load and prepare Iris (3-class, use first 2)
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
X, y = X[y < 2, :4], y[y < 2]  # binary subset
scaler = StandardScaler()
X = scaler.fit_transform(X)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

# Quantum kernel SVM
print("Computing quantum kernel matrices...")
K_train = qsvm_kernel_matrix(X_train[:20], X_train[:20])  # demo subset
K_test  = qsvm_kernel_matrix(X_test[:10],  X_train[:20])

qsvm = SVC(kernel='precomputed', C=1.0)
qsvm.fit(K_train, y_train[:20])
preds = qsvm.predict(K_test)
print(f"QSVM Accuracy: {np.mean(preds == y_test[:10]):.3f}")

# Classical baseline
from sklearn.svm import SVC as ClassicalSVC
classical_svm = ClassicalSVC(kernel='rbf', C=1.0)
classical_svm.fit(X_train[:20], y_train[:20])
print(f"Classical SVM: {classical_svm.score(X_test[:10], y_test[:10]):.3f}")

docs.title: 9.6 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • HHL-QSVM: Exponential speedup claim (Rebentrost 2014) requires qRAM and low condition number. Practical relevance limited.

  • Dequantization: Tang (2019) showed classical algorithms can match HHL-QSVM under the same \(\ell^2\)-norm sampling assumption.

  • QKSVM (practical): Quantum kernel \(\to\) classical SVM optimization. No classical subroutine in the quantum part; \(O(N^2)\) circuit evaluations needed.

  • Multi-class: OvA/OvO strategies standard; direct multi-class via multi-outcome measurements is also possible.

  • Benchmarking: Fair comparisons (Bowles 2024) show no quantum advantage on real datasets. Advantage exists on constructed problems.

Exercises

Exercise . Write out the kernel equation (9.1) for \(N=3\) training points. Identify which matrices appear and their sizes.

Exercise . Show that the quantum kernel SVM decision function \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i\alpha_iy_ik_Q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_i)+b\) lies in the RKHS of the kernel \(k_Q\) (representer theorem).

Exercise . Under what conditions does the condition number \(\kappa\) of the SVM kernel matrix grow with \(N\)? Argue why this is problematic for the HHL-QSVM speedup.

Exercise . Compare QKSVM, classical RBF-SVM, and polynomial-kernel SVM on the Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset. Report accuracy, training time, and kernel matrix condition number.

Further Reading

  • Rebentrost, Mohseni & Lloyd (2014) (Rebentrost et al. 2014) — HHL-QSVM

  • Havlíček et al. (2019) (Havlíček et al. 2019) — quantum kernel SVM on IBM hardware

  • Tang (2019) (Tang 2019) — dequantization of quantum recommendation systems

  • Bowles et al. (2024) (Bowles et al. 2024) — fair benchmarking of quantum classifiers

docs.title: Chapter 10: Quantum Neural Networks
docs.text:
Quantum neural networks (QNNs) generalize deep learning to quantum hardware. The central idea is simple: replace the classical neural network’s layers of matrix multiplications and nonlinearities with layers of parameterized quantum gates. The resulting model is trained by minimizing a quantum expectation value using gradients computed via the parameter shift rule.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Design QNN architectures for classification and regression

  • Derive and apply the parameter shift rule

  • Implement quantum natural gradient (QNG) descent

  • Analyze the expressibility-trainability tradeoff in QNNs

  • Build a complete QNN training loop in PennyLane with PyTorch

docs.title: 10.1 QNN Architecture
docs.text:
A QNN maps data \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) to predictions \(\hat{y}\in\mathbb{R}^K\):

\[\hat{y}_k(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \langle 0|U^\dagger(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\theta})\hat{O}_k U(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\theta})|0\rangle\tag{10.1}\]

The architecture:

\[U(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\theta}) = W_L(\boldsymbol{\theta}_L) S(\mathbf{x}) W_{L-1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{L-1}) \cdots S(\mathbf{x}) W_1(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1)\tag{10.2}\]

where \(S(\mathbf{x})\) encodes the data and \(W_l(\boldsymbol{\theta}_l)\) are trainable unitary layers.

Figure 10.1. QNN architecture: alternating data encoding layers \(S(\mathbf{x})\) and trainable variational layers \(W_l(\boldsymbol{\theta}_l)\), with a final Pauli measurement producing the prediction \(\hat{y}\).

docs.title: 10.2 The Parameter Shift Rule
docs.text:
Theorem 10.1 (Parameter Shift Rule (Mitarai et al. 2018; Schuld et al. 2019))

For a parameterized gate \(U(\theta_i) = e^{-i\theta_i G_i/2}\) where \(G_i\) has eigenvalues \(\pm 1/2\), the gradient of any expectation value is:

\[\frac{\partial\mathcal{C}}{\partial\theta_i} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\mathcal{C}\!\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}+\frac{\pi}{2}\mathbf{e}_i\right) - \mathcal{C}\!\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\frac{\pi}{2}\mathbf{e}_i\right)\right]\tag{10.3}\]

This requires exactly 2 circuit evaluations per parameter and is exact (no finite-difference error).

Solved Example 10.1

Problem: Compute \(\partial\mathcal{C}/\partial\theta\) for \(\mathcal{C}(\theta) = \langle 0|R_y^\dagger(\theta)ZR_y(\theta)|0\rangle\).

Solution: \(R_y(\theta)|0\rangle = \cos(\theta/2)|0\rangle + \sin(\theta/2)|1\rangle\). \(\mathcal{C}(\theta) = \langle Z\rangle = \cos^2(\theta/2)-\sin^2(\theta/2) = \cos\theta\). True gradient: \(\partial\mathcal{C}/\partial\theta = -\sin\theta\).

Parameter shift check: \(\frac{1}{2}[\mathcal{C}(\theta+\pi/2)-\mathcal{C}(\theta-\pi/2)] = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(\theta+\pi/2)-\cos(\theta-\pi/2)] = \frac{1}{2}[-\sin\theta \cdot 2] = -\sin\theta\). ✓

Generalized PSR for gates with eigenvalues \(\pm r/2\):

\[\frac{\partial\mathcal{C}}{\partial\theta_i} = \frac{r}{2}\left[\mathcal{C}\!\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}+\frac{\pi}{2r}\mathbf{e}_i\right) - \mathcal{C}\!\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\frac{\pi}{2r}\mathbf{e}_i\right)\right]\tag{10.4}\]

docs.title: 10.3 Quantum Natural Gradient
docs.text:
Standard gradient descent uses Euclidean metric on parameter space. The Quantum Natural Gradient (QNG) (Stokes et al. 2020) uses the Fubini-Study metric (geometric structure of quantum state space):

\[\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \eta\,\mathbf{F}^+(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\tag{10.5}\]

where \(\mathbf{F}^+\) is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of the QFIM (Eq. (3.9)).

For a parameterized state \(|\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle\):

\[F_{jk}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = 4\,\text{Re}\!\left[\langle\partial_j\psi|\partial_k\psi\rangle - \langle\partial_j\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\partial_k\psi\rangle\right]\]

Solved Example 10.2

Problem: Apply one QNG update to \(|\psi(\theta)\rangle=R_y(\theta)|0\rangle\) with \(\hat{O}=Z\), \(\theta_0=1.0\), \(\eta=0.1\).

Solution: \(\mathcal{C}(\theta)=\cos\theta\), \(\nabla\mathcal{C}=-\sin\theta=-0.841\) at \(\theta=1.0\). QFIM (from Solved Example 3.3): \(F(\theta)=1\). QNG update: \(\theta_1 = 1.0 - 0.1\cdot(1)^{-1}\cdot(-0.841) = 1.0 + 0.084 = 1.084\). For single-parameter circuits, QNG \(\equiv\) GD. Advantage appears with multiple coupled parameters.

Block-diagonal approximation: Full QFIM requires \(O(p^2)\) computations. Approximation with blocks of size 2 (for each gate) reduces to \(O(p)\).

docs.title: 10.4 Loss Functions for QNNs
docs.text:
Binary classification: Hinge loss or cross-entropy on \(\langle Z_0\rangle\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\left[y_i\log\hat{p}_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{p}_i)\right], \quad \hat{p}_i = \sigma\!\left(\langle Z_0\rangle_{\psi_i}\right)\]

Regression: Mean squared error on expectation values:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i\left(\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\psi_i} - y_i\right)^2\]

Multi-class: Softmax over \(K\) observables: \(\hat{p}_k = \text{softmax}_k(\{\langle\hat{O}_j\rangle\}_{j=1}^K)\).

docs.title: 10.5 Expressibility vs. Trainability
docs.text:
Figure 10.2. Left: Train and validation loss curves for a 4-qubit VQC on a toy binary classification task. Right: Optimizer comparison (SGD, Adam, QNG, SPSA, Rotosolve) showing that QNG converges fastest and to the lowest loss. Figure drawn for this book

Important

Fundamental tension: High expressibility requires deep circuits and global entanglement, which leads to barren plateaus (exponentially vanishing gradients). Low expressibility may miss the target function.

Design principle (Cerezo et al. 2021 (Cerezo et al. 2021)): Use local cost functions (few-body observables) and shallow circuits with layerwise training to avoid barren plateaus. See Chapter 16.

docs.title: 10.6 Complete QNN with PennyLane + PyTorch
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml
from pennylane import numpy as pnp
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# -- QNN Device ----------------------------------------------
n_qubits = 4
n_layers = 3
dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits)

@qml.qnode(dev, interface="torch", diff_method="parameter-shift")
def qnn_circuit(inputs, weights):
    """QNN circuit with data re-uploading."""
    for l in range(n_layers):
        # Data encoding (re-upload each layer)
        qml.AngleEmbedding(inputs, wires=range(n_qubits), rotation='Y')
        # Trainable rotation layer
        qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers(weights[l:l+1], wires=range(n_qubits))
    return qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(0))

# -- Hybrid Model ---------------------------------------------
weight_shapes = {"weights": (n_layers, n_qubits, 3)}
qlayer = qml.qnn.TorchLayer(qnn_circuit, weight_shapes)

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, n_qubits),        # Classical pre-processing
    nn.Tanh(),
    qlayer,                         # Quantum layer
    nn.Linear(1, 1),               # Classical post-processing
    nn.Sigmoid()
)

# -- Training -------------------------------------------------
X, y = make_moons(n_samples=100, noise=0.15, random_state=42)
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3)

X_train_t = torch.tensor(X_train, dtype=torch.float32)
y_train_t = torch.tensor(y_train, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1)
X_test_t  = torch.tensor(X_test,  dtype=torch.float32)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
loss_fn   = nn.BCELoss()

print("Training Hybrid QNN...")
for epoch in range(50):
    model.train()
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    preds = model(X_train_t)
    loss = loss_fn(preds, y_train_t)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    if (epoch+1)
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            test_preds = model(X_test_t)
            test_acc = ((test_preds>0.5).float().squeeze().numpy()
                       == y_test).mean()
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1:3d}: loss={loss.item():.4f}, test_acc={test_acc:.3f}")

# -- QNG Optimizer ---------------------------------------------
# PennyLane native QNG:
dev_qng = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=2)
@qml.qnode(dev_qng)
def simple_qnn(params, x):
    qml.AngleEmbedding(x, wires=[0,1])
    qml.RY(params[0], wires=0); qml.RY(params[1], wires=1)
    qml.CNOT(wires=[0,1])
    qml.RY(params[2], wires=0)
    return qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(0))

params = pnp.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3], requires_grad=True)
qng_opt = qml.QNGOptimizer(stepsize=0.1, lam=0.01, approx="block-diag")
x_sample = np.array([0.5, 0.8])
for step in range(5):
    params, cost = qng_opt.step_and_cost(lambda p: simple_qnn(p, x_sample), params)
    print(f"QNG step {step}: cost = {cost:.4f}")

docs.title: 10.7 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • QNN: Data encoding \(+\) parameterized ansatz \(+\) measurement. Output is expectation value \(\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\psi(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\theta})}\).

  • Parameter shift rule: Exact gradient in 2 circuit evaluations per parameter. Key formula: \(\partial_i\mathcal{C} = \frac{1}{2}[\mathcal{C}(\theta_i+\pi/2)-\mathcal{C}(\theta_i-\pi/2)]\).

  • Quantum Natural Gradient: Uses QFIM as metric. Converges faster than vanilla gradient descent. Block-diagonal approximation is practical.

  • Loss functions: BCE, MSE, or cross-entropy applied to expectation values. Multi-class via multiple observables.

  • Expressibility vs. trainability: Fundamental tension. Solution: local cost functions, shallow circuits, and layerwise training.

  • PennyLane-PyTorch: qml.qnn.TorchLayer enables seamless hybrid classical-quantum models with backpropagation.

Exercises

Exercise . Apply the parameter shift rule to compute \(\partial\mathcal{C}/\partial\theta\) for \(\mathcal{C}(\theta) = \langle 0|R_x(\theta)^\dagger X R_x(\theta)|0\rangle\). Verify against the analytic derivative.

Exercise . Show that for a product-state circuit \(U=\bigotimes_i R_y(\theta_i)\) and global observable \(O=Z_0\cdots Z_{n-1}\), the gradient variance scales as \(O(4^{-n})\). (This is the barren plateau for global cost functions.)

Exercise . Derive the QNG update rule from the natural gradient in information geometry. Show that QNG is equivalent to gradient descent in the space of quantum states with respect to the Fubini-Study metric.

Exercise . Implement a QNN for 3-class classification on the Iris dataset. Use 4 qubits, 3 strongly entangling layers, and multi-class output via 3 observables. Report accuracy vs. classical MLP with same number of parameters.

Further Reading

  • Mitarai et al. (2018) (Mitarai et al. 2018) — quantum circuit learning, PSR

  • Schuld et al. (2019) (Schuld et al. 2019) — evaluating analytic gradients on quantum hardware

  • Stokes et al. (2020) (Stokes et al. 2020) — quantum natural gradient

  • Cerezo et al. (2021) (Cerezo et al. 2021) — cost function dependent barren plateaus

docs.title: Chapter 11: Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks
docs.text:
Quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) adapt the inductive biases of classical CNNs — translation equivariance, local feature extraction, and hierarchical pooling — to quantum circuits. They achieve an exponential reduction in trainable parameters compared to general-purpose VQCs and are provably free of barren plateaus. QCNNs have been successfully applied to quantum phase recognition and downscaled image classification.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Explain the QCNN architecture (convolutional + pooling layers)

  • Design translationally invariant quantum convolutional layers

  • Implement measurement-based quantum pooling

  • Apply QCNN to quantum phase recognition (1D Ising model)

  • Build and train a QCNN for image classification in PennyLane

docs.title: 11.1 From CNNs to QCNNs
docs.text:
Classical CNN ingredients and their quantum counterparts:

Table 11.1. CNN vs. QCNN architectural correspondence Classical CNN QCNN Analogue Key Property Pixel values Qubit amplitudes Exponential compression Convolutional filter 2-qubit unitary \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) Translationally invariant Nonlinear activation Born rule measurement Quantum nonlinearity Max/avg pooling Tracing out qubits Qubit reduction Fully connected Global measurement Readout Batch norm (No direct analogue) —

docs.title: 11.2 QCNN Architecture
docs.text:
Figure 11.1. QCNN architecture with 8 input qubits: alternating quantum convolutional layers (parameterised 2-qubit unitaries applied to adjacent pairs) and pooling layers (partial trace, reducing qubits by half). A fully connected measurement layer produces the final class prediction.

The QCNN was introduced by Cong, Choi & Lukin (2019) (Cong et al. 2019). For \(n = 2^k\) qubits, the QCNN has \(k\) alternating convolutional and pooling layers:

Layer structure:

  1. Convolutional layer: Apply the same 2-qubit unitary \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) to all neighboring pairs \((i, i+1)\), then to pairs \((i+1, i+2)\) (with step-1 shift). Same parameters across all sites (translational invariance).

  2. Pooling layer: For each pair of qubits \((i, i+1)\): measure qubit \(i\); apply a classically controlled correction on qubit \(i+1\); discard qubit \(i\). Active qubits are halved at each pooling layer.

Parameter count: \(\log_2(n)\) layers \(\times\) \(O(1)\) parameters per layer \(= O(\log n)\) total (vs. \(O(n \cdot L)\) for hardware-efficient ansatz).

Note

The \(O(\log n)\) parameter count is both a feature (tractable optimization) and a limitation (limited expressibility). QCNNs are best suited for tasks with inherent hierarchical structure, like quantum phases of matter.

docs.title: 11.3 Quantum Convolutional Layers
docs.text:
The 2-qubit convolutional kernel \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) can be any general 2-qubit unitary parameterized by \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{15}\) (15 independent parameters for \(SU(4)\)). Common choices:

  • General \(SU(4)\): Full expressibility but many parameters

  • Ansatz with specific structure: \(R_{ZZ}R_{YY}R_{XX}\) (Ising-inspired)

  • Nearest-neighbor: \(R_{ZZ}(\theta_1)R_y(\theta_2)R_y(\theta_3)\) followed by CNOT

Translational invariance: Same \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) for all pairs — exactly \(d\) parameters per convolutional layer (where \(d\) is the gate’s dimension).

docs.title: 11.4 Quantum Pooling Layers
docs.text:
Measurement-based pooling:

  1. Measure qubit \(i\) in the computational basis; outcome \(m\in\{0,1\}\)

  2. Apply classical feedback on qubit \(i+1\): \(X^m\) correction (or more general unitary)

  3. Discard qubit \(i\) from the active register

This is the quantum analogue of max-pooling: the “strongest” information is propagated to the next layer via classical feedback.

Solved Example 11.1

Problem: Trace through 1 QCNN layer on 4 qubits in state \(|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0000\rangle + \beta|1111\rangle\).

Solution: After convolution \(U\) on pairs \((0,1)\), \((1,2)\), \((2,3)\) (simplified as identity here): state unchanged.

Pooling on pair \((0,1)\): Measure qubit 0.

  • With probability \(|\alpha|^2\): outcome 0, qubit 1 remains in state \(\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\) (for Bell-like \(|\psi\rangle\): actually need to trace through carefully)

  • With probability \(|\beta|^2\): outcome 1, apply \(X\) to qubit 1

After pooling: 2 active qubits remain. The information from qubits 0,2 is transferred to qubits 1,3.

docs.title: 11.5 QCNN for Quantum Phase Recognition
docs.text:
Application: Classify quantum phases of the 1D transverse-field Ising model:

\[\hat{H}(h) = -J\sum_i Z_i Z_{i+1} - h\sum_i X_i\tag{11.1}\]

Phase transition at \(h/J = 1\): ferromagnetic (\(h<J\)) vs. paramagnetic (\(h>J\)) phase.

Training: Input ground states \(|\psi_{\text{GS}}(h)\rangle\); labels: phase. QCNN output \(\langle Z_0\rangle\) close to \(\pm 1\) for the two phases.

Cong et al. (2019) showed QCNN achieves \(>99\%\) accuracy with only \(O(\log n)\) parameters and no barren plateaus.

docs.title: 11.6 QCNN for Image Classification
docs.text:
Approach for MNIST: downsample to \(4\times4 = 16\) pixels \(\to\) 16 qubits via amplitude encoding.

  1. Flatten and normalize \(4\times4\) image to unit vector \(\mathbf{x}/\|\mathbf{x}\|\)

  2. Amplitude encode: \(|\phi\rangle = \sum_i x_i|i\rangle\) (16 qubits? \(\to\) 4 qubits via \(\log_2(16)=4\)!)

  3. Apply QCNN: 2 convolutional + 2 pooling layers, ending with 1 qubit

  4. Measure final qubit: \(\langle Z\rangle > 0 \to\) class 0, \(\langle Z\rangle < 0 \to\) class 1

import pennylane as qml
from pennylane import numpy as pnp
import numpy as np

n_qubits = 8  # 8-qubit QCNN (3 pooling layers -> 1 qubit)
dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits)

def conv_layer(params, wires):
    """Single convolutional layer: U(params) applied translationally."""
    n = len(wires)
    for i in range(0, n-1, 2):  # even pairs
        qml.IsingXX(params[0], wires=[wires[i], wires[i+1]])
        qml.IsingYY(params[1], wires=[wires[i], wires[i+1]])
        qml.IsingZZ(params[2], wires=[wires[i], wires[i+1]])
    for i in range(1, n-1, 2):  # odd pairs
        qml.IsingXX(params[0], wires=[wires[i], wires[i+1]])
        qml.IsingYY(params[1], wires=[wires[i], wires[i+1]])
        qml.IsingZZ(params[2], wires=[wires[i], wires[i+1]])

def pool_layer(params, sources, sinks):
    """Pooling: measure sources, classically-conditioned correction on sinks."""
    for source, sink in zip(sources, sinks):
        # Simplified: controlled-unitary from source to sink
        qml.CNOT(wires=[source, sink])
        qml.RZ(params[0], wires=sink)
        qml.CNOT(wires=[source, sink])

@qml.qnode(dev)
def qcnn_circuit(data, conv_params, pool_params):
    """QCNN with 3 conv+pool layers for 8 -> 1 qubit."""
    # Data encoding (amplitude embedding)
    qml.AmplitudeEmbedding(data, wires=range(n_qubits), normalize=True)

    # Layer 1: Conv on all 8 qubits, pool 8->4
    conv_layer(conv_params[0], list(range(8)))
    pool_layer(pool_params[0], [0,2,4,6], [1,3,5,7])
    active = [1, 3, 5, 7]

    # Layer 2: Conv on 4 qubits, pool 4->2
    conv_layer(conv_params[1], active)
    pool_layer(pool_params[1], [1,5], [3,7])
    active = [3, 7]

    # Layer 3: Conv on 2 qubits, pool 2->1
    conv_layer(conv_params[2], active)
    pool_layer(pool_params[2], [3], [7])

    return qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(7))  # final qubit measurement

# Initialize parameters
conv_params = pnp.random.randn(3, 3, requires_grad=True)  # 3 layers x 3 params
pool_params  = pnp.random.randn(3, 1, requires_grad=True)  # 3 layers x 1 param

# Test forward pass
x = np.random.randn(2**n_qubits)
x = x / np.linalg.norm(x)
output = qcnn_circuit(x, conv_params, pool_params)
print(f"QCNN output: {output:.4f}  (total params: {3*3 + 3*1} = 12)")

# Training loop
opt = qml.AdamOptimizer(stepsize=0.1)
# Combine params for optimizer
all_params = [conv_params, pool_params]
for step in range(20):
    loss = lambda cp, pp: (qcnn_circuit(x, cp, pp) - 0.5)**2
    conv_params, pool_params = opt.step(
        lambda cp, pp: loss(cp, pp), conv_params, pool_params)
    if step
        print(f"Step {step}: loss = {loss(conv_params, pool_params):.6f}")

docs.title: 11.7 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • QCNN = quantum convolutional layers (shared 2-qubit unitaries, translationally invariant) + pooling layers (measure half the qubits each step).

  • Parameter count: \(O(\log n)\) — exponentially fewer than generic VQC.

  • No barren plateaus: Local convolutional structure and logarithmic depth provably prevent exponentially vanishing gradients.

  • Applications: Quantum phase recognition (Ising model) and downscaled image classification. Performance competitive with classical CNNs for the same input size.

  • Limitation: Only works well for hierarchically structured data; does not generalize to arbitrary classification tasks.

Exercises

Exercise . For an \(n=8\) qubit QCNN with the architecture described in this chapter, how many convolutional and pooling layers are needed? How many total parameters?

Exercise . Show that the measurement-based pooling is equivalent to tracing out the measured qubit from the density matrix, post-selected on the measurement outcome.

Exercise . Prove that QCNN gradients with local cost functions do not vanish exponentially with \(n\). Hint: Follow the argument of Cerezo et al. (2021).

Exercise . Implement a 4-qubit QCNN for binary classification of \(2\times2\) images (encoded as 4-qubit states). Train on a synthetic image dataset and plot the training curve.

Further Reading

  • Cong, Choi & Lukin (2019) (Cong et al. 2019) — original QCNN paper

  • Pesah et al. (2021) — absence of barren plateaus in QCNNs

  • Hur et al. (2022) — quantum convolutional neural network for classical data

docs.title: Chapter 12: Quantum Recurrent Networks and QLSTM
docs.text:
Sequence modeling is central to NLP, time series analysis, and control. Classical RNNs and LSTMs process sequences by maintaining a hidden state that is updated at each timestep. Quantum analogues replace the classical hidden state and gate operations with quantum states and parameterized quantum circuits, potentially enabling richer memory and expressibility.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Describe the QLSTM architecture and its gate operations

  • Distinguish quantum and classical components of the hybrid model

  • Implement a QLSTM in PennyLane for sequence classification

  • Apply quantum reservoir computing (QRC) for temporal tasks

  • Benchmark QLSTM against classical LSTM on sequence datasets

docs.title: 12.1 Classical LSTM Review
docs.text:
An LSTM processes sequence \((\mathbf{x}_1,…,\mathbf{x}_T)\) via:

\[\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f[\mathbf{h}_{t-1},\mathbf{x}_t]+\mathbf{b}_f) \quad\text{(forget gate)} \\ \mathbf{i}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}_i[\mathbf{h}_{t-1},\mathbf{x}_t]+\mathbf{b}_i) \quad\text{(input gate)} \\ \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t &= \tanh(\mathbf{W}_c[\mathbf{h}_{t-1},\mathbf{x}_t]+\mathbf{b}_c) \quad\text{(cell update)} \\ \mathbf{c}_t &= \mathbf{f}_t\odot\mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t\odot\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t \quad\text{(cell state)} \\ \mathbf{o}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}_o[\mathbf{h}_{t-1},\mathbf{x}_t]+\mathbf{b}_o) \quad\text{(output gate)} \\ \mathbf{h}_t &= \mathbf{o}_t\odot\tanh(\mathbf{c}_t) \quad\text{(hidden state)} \end{align*}\]

The gates control information flow via sigmoid activations. Vanishing gradients in deep RNNs are mitigated by the cell state \(\mathbf{c}_t\).

docs.title: 12.2 QLSTM Architecture
docs.text:
Figure 12.1. QLSTM cell: the four classical LSTM gate networks (\(f\), \(i\), \(g\), \(o\)) are replaced by parameterised quantum circuits (VQCs). The classical linear projection maps the concatenated input \([\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}]\) into qubit rotation angles; the VQC outputs are then passed through classical activation functions to produce the updated cell state \(\mathbf{c}_t\) and hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_t\).

The Quantum LSTM (Chen et al., 2022) (Chen et al. 2022) replaces the classical linear transformations \(\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{h},\mathbf{x}]+\mathbf{b}\) in each gate with a parameterized quantum circuit:

\[\text{VQC}_{\text{gate}}(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{gate}}) = \langle\hat{O}\rangle_{U(\boldsymbol{\theta})|\phi(\mathbf{x}_t,\mathbf{h}_{t-1})\rangle}\tag{12.7}\]

QLSTM equations (replacing linear layers with VQCs):

\[\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}_t &= \sigma(\text{VQC}_f(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_f)) \\ \mathbf{i}_t &= \sigma(\text{VQC}_i(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_i)) \\ \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t &= \tanh(\text{VQC}_c(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_c)) \\ \mathbf{c}_t &= \mathbf{f}_t\odot\mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t\odot\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t \\ \mathbf{o}_t &= \sigma(\text{VQC}_o(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_o)) \\ \mathbf{h}_t &= \mathbf{o}_t\odot\tanh(\mathbf{c}_t) \end{align*}\]

Each VQC gate has its own parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{gate}}\). The cell state \(\mathbf{c}_t\) and hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_t\) remain classical vectors.

Tip

The QLSTM is a hybrid architecture: quantum circuits compute gate activations, but the state update logic (equations for \(\mathbf{c}_t\), \(\mathbf{h}_t\)) is purely classical. This is practical on NISQ hardware since only small quantum circuits are needed.

docs.title: 12.3 VQC Gate Design for QLSTM
docs.text:
Each VQC gate receives concatenated input \([\mathbf{x}_t; \mathbf{h}_{t-1}]\) and returns scalar outputs (one per hidden dimension \(h\)):

Input encoding: Angle encoding on \(n_{\text{in}}\) qubits:

Solved Example 12.1

Problem: For a 2-qubit QLSTM forget gate with angle encoding of \([x_t, h_{t-1}]\) and 1 strongly entangling layer, how many parameters does the gate have?

Solution: Strongly entangling layer on 2 qubits: \(2\times3 = 6\) parameters (each qubit gets 3 rotation angles: \(R_z R_y R_z\)). Plus CNOT: no parameters. Total per gate: \(6\) parameters. For 4 QLSTM gates (f, i, c, o): \(4\times6=24\) parameters.

Classical LSTM equivalent: for hidden size \(h=2\) and input size \(d=1\): \(4\times(h\cdot(h+d)+h) = 4\times(2\cdot3+2)=32\) parameters. QLSTM uses fewer parameters but requires 4 quantum circuit evaluations per timestep.

docs.title: 12.4 Quantum Reservoir Computing
docs.text:
Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) (Fujii and Nakajima 2017) is a simpler alternative to QLSTM: use a fixed (non-trainable) random quantum circuit as the reservoir, and train only a classical readout layer.

Architecture:

  1. Input: Encode \(\mathbf{x}_t\) into initial qubit rotations

  2. Reservoir: Apply fixed random entangling unitary \(U\) (not trained)

  3. Readout: Measure all qubits, apply trained linear readout \(\mathbf{W}_{\text{out}}\)

Memory capacity: The quantum system retains memory of past inputs through its entangled state. For an \(n\)-qubit reservoir, memory capacity \(\propto n\).

Note

QRC requires no quantum gradient computation — only the classical readout is trained. This makes it extremely hardware-friendly and gradient-free. However, it cannot be fine-tuned for specific tasks as well as trained QLSTM.

docs.title: 12.5 Implementation
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

n_qubits_in = 4
dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits_in)

@qml.qnode(dev, interface="torch", diff_method="parameter-shift")
def vqc_gate(inputs, weights):
    """VQC for one QLSTM gate (forget/input/output/cell)."""
    qml.AngleEmbedding(inputs, wires=range(n_qubits_in), rotation='Y')
    qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers(weights, wires=range(n_qubits_in))
    return [qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(i)) for i in range(n_qubits_in)]

weight_shape = {"weights": (2, n_qubits_in, 3)}

class QLSTMCell(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, n_qubits=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        # One VQC per gate
        self.vqc_f = qml.qnn.TorchLayer(vqc_gate, weight_shape)
        self.vqc_i = qml.qnn.TorchLayer(vqc_gate, weight_shape)
        self.vqc_c = qml.qnn.TorchLayer(vqc_gate, weight_shape)
        self.vqc_o = qml.qnn.TorchLayer(vqc_gate, weight_shape)
        # Classical projections
        self.proj_in = nn.Linear(input_size + hidden_size, n_qubits)
        self.proj_out = nn.Linear(n_qubits, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, x, hidden):
        h, c = hidden
        combined = torch.cat([x, h], dim=-1)
        q_input = torch.tanh(self.proj_in(combined)) * np.pi  # scale to [-pi, pi]
        # Quantum gate evaluations
        f = torch.sigmoid(self.proj_out(self.vqc_f(q_input)))
        i = torch.sigmoid(self.proj_out(self.vqc_i(q_input)))
        g = torch.tanh(  self.proj_out(self.vqc_c(q_input)))
        o = torch.sigmoid(self.proj_out(self.vqc_o(q_input)))
        # Cell state update
        c_new = f * c + i * g
        h_new = o * torch.tanh(c_new)
        return h_new, (h_new, c_new)

class QLSTMClassifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size=1, hidden_size=4, n_classes=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.cell = QLSTMCell(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_size, n_classes)

    def forward(self, seq):
        # seq: (batch, time, features)
        B, T, _ = seq.shape
        h = torch.zeros(B, self.hidden_size)
        c = torch.zeros(B, self.hidden_size)
        for t in range(T):
            h, (h, c) = self.cell(seq[:, t, :], (h, c))
        return self.fc(h)  # classify on final hidden state

# Quick test
model = QLSTMClassifier(input_size=1, hidden_size=4, n_classes=2)
x = torch.randn(4, 10, 1)  # batch=4, seq_len=10, features=1
print("QLSTM output shape:", model(x).shape)
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Total parameters: {n_params}")

docs.title: 12.6 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • QLSTM: Each LSTM gate (forget/input/cell/output) is replaced by a VQC. Cell state and hidden state remain classical. Hybrid architecture.

  • Training: BPTT through the classical cell state + PSR for VQC gradients. 4 VQC evaluations per timestep per gate.

  • Expressibility: VQC gates can represent richer nonlinear functions than classical sigmoid/tanh in some regimes.

  • QRC: Fixed random quantum circuit as reservoir; only classical readout trained. Gradient-free and hardware-friendly.

  • Applications: NLP (sentence classification), time series forecasting, quantum state tomography sequences.

Exercises

Exercise . Draw the QLSTM architecture diagram showing the 4 VQC gates, classical cell state update, and hidden state output for one timestep.

Exercise . Compare the number of parameters for a classical LSTM with hidden size \(h=8\), input size \(d=2\) vs. a QLSTM with 4-qubit gates and same hidden size.

Exercise . Train a QLSTM for the task of classifying whether a sine wave sequence has frequency above or below 0.5 Hz. Generate 200 sequences of length 20. Compare with a 2-layer classical GRU.

Further Reading

  • Chen et al. (2022) (Chen et al. 2022) — QLSTM for sequence learning

  • Fujii & Nakajima (2017) (Fujii and Nakajima 2017) — quantum reservoir computing

  • Bausch (2020) — recurrent quantum neural networks

docs.title: Chapter 13: Quantum Autoencoders
docs.text:
Autoencoders learn compact representations of data by compressing it through a bottleneck and reconstructing the original. Quantum autoencoders (QAEs) generalize this to quantum states: a parameterized quantum circuit compresses an \(n\)-qubit state into \(k < n\) qubits (latent space), discarding the rest, and a decoder recovers the original state. Applications span quantum state compression, noise filtering, anomaly detection, and quantum memory.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Explain the quantum autoencoder architecture of Romero et al. (2017)

  • Derive the SWAP-test and Hilbert–Schmidt inner product training objectives

  • Implement a QAE in PennyLane for pure-state compression

  • Apply QAEs to denoising and anomaly detection on quantum states

  • Analyse the information-theoretic limits of quantum data compression

docs.title: 13.1 Classical Autoencoders: A Brief Review
docs.text:
A classical autoencoder comprises an encoder \(f_\phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) and a decoder \(g_\psi:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}^n\) (\(k < n\)), trained to minimise the reconstruction loss:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{AE}} = \mathbb{E}_x\bigl[\|x - g_\psi(f_\phi(x))\|^2\bigr]\tag{13.1}\]

The bottleneck forces the network to learn a low-dimensional latent representation \(z = f_\phi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^k\) capturing the essential structure of the data distribution.

Variational autoencoders (VAEs) extend this by learning a latent distribution \(q_\phi(z|x)\approx p(z|x)\), enabling generative sampling. Quantum analogues of both exist; this chapter focuses on the compression/ denoising variant.

docs.title: 13.2 Quantum Autoencoder Architecture
docs.text:
Definition: Quantum Autoencoder (Romero et al., 2017)

A quantum autoencoder (QAE) for \(n\)-qubit input states consists of:

  1. Encoder: parameterized unitary \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) acting on \(n\) qubits.

  2. Latent space: \(k\) qubits retained (the “latent” register).

  3. Trash register: \(n-k\) qubits discarded (traced out).

  4. Decoder: \(U^\dagger(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) – the inverse encoder acting on latent + \(n-k\) reference qubits.

The key insight of Romero et al. (Romero et al. 2017): the decoder need not be separately parameterized – it is simply the conjugate transpose of the encoder \(U^\dagger\). This makes the QAE symmetric.

Architecture diagram (for \(n=3\), \(k=1\)):

After encoding, the trash qubits should be in a fixed reference state \(|0\rangle^{\otimes(n-k)}\) for perfect compression. The training objective maximises the overlap between the trash qubits and \(|0\rangle\).

docs.title: 13.3.1 Fidelity-Based Loss
docs.text:
For a pure input state \(|\psi\rangle\), after encoding:

\[U(\boldsymbol{\theta})|\psi\rangle|\mathbf{0}\rangle = |\phi_{\text{latent}}\rangle \otimes |\text{trash}\rangle\]

Training objective: maximise the overlap of the trash register with the reference state \(|0\rangle^{\otimes(n-k)}\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{QAE}} = 1 - \bigl|\langle 0|^{\otimes(n-k)}\,\rho_{\text{trash}}\,|0\rangle^{\otimes(n-k)}\bigr|\tag{13.3}\]

where \(\rho_{\text{trash}} = \mathrm{Tr}_{\text{latent}}[U|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|U^\dagger]\).

docs.title: 13.3.2 SWAP-Test Fidelity
docs.text:
An alternative formulation uses the SWAP test to measure fidelity between the original input and the reconstructed output:

\[F(\rho, \sigma) = \mathrm{Tr}[\rho\sigma] = \langle\psi|U^\dagger\Pi_{\text{ref}}U|\psi\rangle\]

where \(\Pi_{\text{ref}} = |0\rangle\langle 0|^{\otimes(n-k)}\otimes I_k\).

The SWAP-test ancilla measurement yields probability \(P(0) = \frac{1}{2}(1 + \langle\psi|\sigma|\psi\rangle)\), so \(F = 2P(0) - 1\).

docs.title: 13.3.3 Hilbert–Schmidt Inner Product (Mixed States)
docs.text:
For mixed-state inputs \(\rho\) (e.g. noisy states):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{HS}} = 1 - \mathrm{Tr}[\rho\,\sigma]\tag{13.5}\]

where \(\sigma = \mathcal{D}\circ\mathcal{E}(\rho)\) is the decoded state after encoding. This is estimated via the destructive SWAP test.

Solved Example 13.1

Problem: For a 3-qubit QAE compressing to 1 qubit, what is the maximum compression ratio, and what is the information-theoretic requirement on the input ensemble for perfect compression?
