Solution: Compression ratio \(= n/k = 3/1 = 3\times\). The input space is \(2^3=8\)-dimensional, the latent space is \(2^1=2\)-dimensional.

By Schumacher compression (Schumacher 1995), perfect quantum compression to \(k\) qubits is possible if and only if the input ensemble \(\{p_i, |\psi_i\rangle\}\) has von Neumann entropy \(S(\rho) \leq k\) qubits, where \(\rho = \sum_i p_i |\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|\).

If \(S(\rho) > k\), information is necessarily lost. The QAE loss equals \(S(\rho) - k\) qubits of lost information in the optimal case.

For a 3-qubit maximally mixed state \(\rho = I/8\), \(S(\rho) = 3\) bits, so compression to 1 qubit necessarily loses 2 qubits of information – perfect reconstruction is impossible.

docs.title: 13.4 Encoder Ansatz Design
docs.text:
The encoder \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) must be expressive enough to learn the optimal compression. Common choices:

Algorithm: QAE Encoder Ansatz

  1. Strongly entangling layers: \(L\) layers of single-qubit rotations + CNOT ladders. Parameters: \(3Ln\) per layer.

  2. Hardware-efficient ansatz: matches device connectivity.

  3. Problem-inspired: exploit known structure (e.g. translation invariance for periodic quantum states).

Circuit depth: For \(n\)-qubit inputs, \(O(n^2)\) two-qubit gates suffice to implement any unitary (via KAK decomposition).

docs.title: 13.5 Quantum State Denoising
docs.text:
A QAE trained on pure states can act as a quantum denoiser: given a noisy state \(\mathcal{N}(\rho)\) (depolarizing, dephasing, amplitude damping), the encoder finds a latent representation that filters out noise.

Procedure:

  1. Prepare training pairs: \((|\psi_i\rangle,\, \mathcal{N}(|\psi_i\rangle))\)

  2. Train QAE to compress \(\mathcal{N}(|\psi_i\rangle)\) and reconstruct \(|\psi_i\rangle\)

  3. At inference: apply encoder + decoder to noisy input

Note

Quantum state denoising via QAE differs from quantum error correction (QEC): QEC uses syndrome measurements and is exact; QAE denoising is variational and approximate but works on NISQ hardware without ancilla overhead.

docs.title: 13.6 Anomaly Detection with QAE
docs.text:
Figure 13.1. Left: Reconstruction fidelity vs training epochs for four QAE compression configurations. Right: ROC curves for anomaly detection, comparing the QAE (AUC \(\approx 0.91\)) with a classical autoencoder and random baseline. Figure drawn for this book

A QAE trained on “normal” quantum states will reconstruct normal states well but fail on anomalous ones. The reconstruction error serves as an anomaly score:

\[\text{score}(|\psi\rangle) = 1 - F(|\psi\rangle,\, \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{E}(|\psi\rangle)))\tag{13.6}\]

Applications:

  • Quantum hardware calibration: detect drifting qubits via state anomaly

  • Quantum chemistry: identify anomalous molecular configurations

  • Quantum communication: detect eavesdropping via state perturbation detection

docs.title: 13.7 Implementation
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# QAE: 4 qubits -> 2 qubit latent space
n_qubits = 4
n_latent = 2
n_trash  = n_qubits - n_latent  # 2 trash qubits
n_layers = 3

dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits)

@qml.qnode(dev, interface="torch", diff_method="parameter-shift")
def qae_circuit(state_params, enc_weights):
    """
    QAE circuit: encode target state, apply encoder U(theta),
    measure fidelity of trash qubits with |0>.
    state_params: angles for preparing input state
    enc_weights:  encoder ansatz parameters shape (n_layers, n_qubits, 3)
    """
    # Prepare input state (angle encoding)
    qml.AngleEmbedding(state_params, wires=range(n_qubits), rotation='Y')
    # Encoder: strongly entangling layers
    qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers(enc_weights, wires=range(n_qubits))
    # Measure trash qubits (want them to be |0>)
    return [qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(i)) for i in range(n_latent, n_qubits)]

def qae_loss(state_params, enc_weights):
    """
    Loss = 1 - fidelity_of_trash_with_0.
    expval PauliZ = 1 if |0>, -1 if |1>.
    Fidelity with |0> = (1 + <Z>) / 2 for each qubit.
    """
    z_vals = qae_circuit(state_params, enc_weights)
    fidels = [(1 + z) / 2 for z in z_vals]
    avg_fid = sum(fidels) / n_trash
    return 1 - avg_fid

@qml.qnode(dev, interface="torch")
def full_autoencoder(state_params, enc_weights):
    """Encode + decode (U^dag) to reconstruct original state."""
    # Prepare input
    qml.AngleEmbedding(state_params, wires=range(n_qubits), rotation='Y')
    # Encode
    qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers(enc_weights, wires=range(n_qubits))
    # Reset trash qubits (set to |0> reference)
    for w in range(n_latent, n_qubits):
        qml.PauliX(w)  # simple reset approximation
        qml.PauliX(w)
    # Decode = U^dagger
    qml.adjoint(qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers)(enc_weights,
                                              wires=range(n_qubits))
    return qml.state()

# Training
weight_shape = (n_layers, n_qubits, 3)
enc_weights = torch.tensor(
    np.random.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi, weight_shape),
    dtype=torch.float32, requires_grad=True
)

# Training data: 20 random 4-qubit states (described by 4 angle params each)
np.random.seed(42)
train_states = torch.tensor(
    np.random.uniform(0, np.pi, (20, n_qubits)), dtype=torch.float32
)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([enc_weights], lr=0.05)

print("Training QAE...")
for epoch in range(100):
    total_loss = 0.0
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    for s in train_states:
        loss = qae_loss(s, enc_weights)
        total_loss += loss
    total_loss = total_loss / len(train_states)
    total_loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    if (epoch + 1)
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1:3d} | Loss: {total_loss.item():.4f} "
              f"| Fidelity: {1-total_loss.item():.4f}")

# Evaluate compression fidelity on new state
test_state = torch.tensor([0.8, 1.2, 0.4, 1.7])
loss_val = qae_loss(test_state, enc_weights)
print(f"\nTest compression fidelity: {1 - loss_val.item():.4f}")

# Anomaly detection demo
normal_state  = torch.tensor([0.9, 1.1, 0.5, 1.6])
anomaly_state = torch.tensor([np.pi, np.pi, np.pi, np.pi])  # distinct
score_normal  = qae_loss(normal_state,  enc_weights).item()
score_anomaly = qae_loss(anomaly_state, enc_weights).item()
print(f"Anomaly score (normal):  {score_normal:.4f}")
print(f"Anomaly score (anomaly): {score_anomaly:.4f}")

docs.title: 13.8 Information-Theoretic Limits
docs.text:
Definition: Schumacher Compression

For an ensemble \(\{p_i, |\psi_i\rangle\}\) with density matrix \(\rho = \sum_i p_i|\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|\), Schumacher’s quantum source coding theorem (Schumacher 1995) states:

The minimum number of qubits required for reliable compression is \(S(\rho) = -\mathrm{Tr}[\rho\log_2\rho]\) (von Neumann entropy).

A QAE achieves this limit when \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) converges to the optimal compression unitary that maps the principal eigenvectors of \(\rho\) to the latent register and discards the rest.

Tip

The QAE encoder finds, via gradient descent, an approximation to the typical subspace of the input ensemble – the quantum analogue of Shannon’s typical sequences. The latent register spans the most probable subspace of \(\rho\).

docs.title: 13.9 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • QAE architecture: Encoder \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) compresses \(n\) qubits to \(k\) latent qubits; decoder is \(U^\dagger\). Symmetric by design.

  • Training: Maximise fidelity of trash register with \(|0\rangle\) via SWAP test or Pauli-Z expectation values. Gradient via PSR.

  • Denoising: Train on noisy/clean pairs; reconstruction error filters noise from quantum states.

  • Anomaly detection: High reconstruction error \(\Rightarrow\) anomalous state. Useful for hardware calibration and security.

  • Fundamental limits: Schumacher’s theorem gives the von Neumann entropy as the minimal qubit compression bound.

Exercises

Exercise . Explain why the QAE decoder is simply \(U^\dagger(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) and not a separately parameterized circuit. What condition on the input ensemble allows this to work?

Exercise . For a 4-qubit QAE compressing to 2 qubits, derive the maximum number of linearly independent input states that can be perfectly compressed. How does this relate to the Hilbert-space dimension?

Exercise . Implement a quantum state denoiser using the QAE above: generate 50 random 2-qubit pure states, apply depolarizing noise (\(p=0.1\)), train the QAE to reconstruct the clean states, and plot reconstruction fidelity vs. noise strength.

Further Reading

  • Romero et al. (2017) (Romero et al. 2017) — original QAE proposal

  • Schumacher (1995) (Schumacher 1995) — quantum source coding theorem

  • Pepper et al. (2019) — QAE for mixed states and denoising

  • Cao & Babbush (2024) — QAE benchmarks on near-term hardware

docs.title: Chapter 14: Quantum Generative Models
docs.text:
Generative modelling aims to learn and sample from a data distribution. Classical counterparts — GANs, VAEs, normalizing flows — have achieved remarkable success. Quantum generative models leverage quantum superposition and entanglement to represent distributions that may be hard to capture classically. This chapter covers Quantum GANs (QGANs), Born machines, and Quantum Boltzmann Machines (QBMs).

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Describe the QGAN architecture and its training adversarial objective

  • Implement a Born machine and train it via maximum mean discrepancy

  • Explain Quantum Boltzmann Machines and their thermal sampling

  • Compare quantum and classical generative models in terms of expressibility

  • Apply QGANs to generate quantum state distributions in PennyLane

docs.title: 14.1.1 Classical GAN Review
docs.text:
A GAN (Goodfellow et al. 2014) comprises:

  • Generator \(G_\theta: z\mapsto x'\) – maps noise to fake samples

  • Discriminator \(D_\phi: x\mapsto[0,1]\) – classifies real vs. fake

Minimax objective:

\[\min_\theta\max_\phi\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_\text{data}}[\log D_\phi(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_z}[\log(1-D_\phi(G_\theta(z)))]\tag{14.1}\]

docs.title: 14.1.2 QGAN Architecture
docs.text:
The Quantum GAN (Lloyd & Weedbrook, 2018; Dallaire-Demers & Killoran, 2018) (Lloyd and Weedbrook 2018; Dallaire-Demers and Killoran 2018) replaces the generator (or both components) with parameterized quantum circuits:

Quantum generator: A PQC \(G(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) acting on \(|0\rangle^n\) produces state \(\sigma(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = G|\mathbf{0}\rangle\langle\mathbf{0}|G^\dagger\).

Quantum discriminator: A PQC \(D(\boldsymbol{\phi})\) followed by a single-qubit measurement estimates the probability that the input is real:

\[D_\phi(\rho) = \mathrm{Tr}[\Pi_1 D(\boldsymbol{\phi})\rho D^\dagger(\boldsymbol{\phi})]\tag{14.2}\]

docs.title: 14.1.3 QGAN Training Objective
docs.text:
\[\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\max_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\; \mathrm{Tr}[\Pi_1 D_\phi \rho_\text{data}] - \mathrm{Tr}[\Pi_1 D_\phi \sigma_\theta]\tag{14.3}\]

This is the quantum analogue of the Wasserstein GAN objective, measuring the trace distance between real and generated quantum state distributions.

Solved Example 14.1

Problem: A 2-qubit QGAN generator applies \(R_y(\theta_1)R_y(\theta_2)\) followed by a CNOT. What distribution over computational basis states does it produce for \(\theta_1=\pi/4\), \(\theta_2=0\)?

Solution: Initial state: \(|00\rangle\). After \(R_y(\pi/4)\otimes R_y(0)\): \(|00\rangle\to(\cos\frac{\pi}{8}|0\rangle+\sin\frac{\pi}{8}|1\rangle)\otimes|0\rangle\).

After CNOT (control=qubit 0, target=qubit 1): \(\cos\frac{\pi}{8}|00\rangle + \sin\frac{\pi}{8}|11\rangle\) (a Bell-like state).

Distribution: \(P(00) = \cos^2\frac{\pi}{8} \approx 0.854\), \(P(11) = \sin^2\frac{\pi}{8} \approx 0.146\), all others \(= 0\).

This generator produces entangled outputs, unlike a separable classical neural network generator.

docs.title: 14.2 Born Machines
docs.text:
Definition: Born Machine

A Born machine (Liu and Wang 2018) is a quantum circuit \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) whose measurement outcome distribution

\[p_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = |\langle\mathbf{x}|U(\boldsymbol{\theta})|0\rangle^n|^2\tag{14.4}\]

is trained to match a target distribution \(q(\mathbf{x})\) over bitstrings \(\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^n\).

The Born rule naturally produces a valid probability distribution over \(2^n\) bitstrings, making the Born machine a natural quantum generative model.

docs.title: 14.2.1 Training via Maximum Mean Discrepancy
docs.text:
The Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between \(p_\theta\) and \(q\) is:

\[\text{MMD}^2(p_\theta, q) = \mathbb{E}_{x,x'\sim p_\theta}[k(x,x')] - 2\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_\theta, y\sim q}[k(x,y)] + \mathbb{E}_{y,y'\sim q}[k(y,y')]\tag{14.5}\]

where \(k(\cdot,\cdot)\) is a kernel (e.g. Gaussian or Hamming kernel on bitstrings).

MMD gradient via PSR: The gradient \(\partial_\theta\,\text{MMD}^2\) can be estimated using parameter-shift rules on the quantum circuit.

docs.title: 14.2.2 Expressibility of Born Machines
docs.text:
Born machines can represent distributions that are hard classically:

Important

Quantum advantage for generation: Liu & Rebentrost (2018) showed that certain Born machines with depth-\(O(\log n)\) circuits can sample from distributions that require \(\Omega(n^{1/4})\)-depth classical circuits. Specifically, output distributions of random quantum circuits (RQCs) are believed to be classically hard (quantum supremacy experiments).

docs.title: 14.3 Quantum Boltzmann Machines
docs.text:
Definition: Quantum Boltzmann Machine (QBM)

A Quantum Boltzmann Machine (Amin et al. 2018) is a generative model whose distribution is defined by a quantum Hamiltonian:

\[\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{e^{-H(\boldsymbol{\theta})/T}}{Z(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\tag{14.6}\]

where \(Z(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathrm{Tr}[e^{-H(\boldsymbol{\theta})/T}]\) is the partition function, \(T\) is temperature, and \(H(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) is a parameterized quantum Hamiltonian.

Hamiltonian structure:

\[H(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\sum_i h_i Z_i - \sum_{i<j} J_{ij}Z_iZ_j - \Gamma\sum_i X_i\tag{14.7}\]

where \(h_i, J_{ij}\) are bias/coupling parameters (classical RBM terms) and \(\Gamma\) is a transverse field (quantum term enabling quantum tunneling).

docs.title: 14.3.1 Training QBMs
docs.text:
The log-likelihood gradient for a QBM:

\[\frac{\partial\log p_\theta(\mathbf{v})}{\partial\theta_k} = \langle O_k\rangle_{\rho_\mathbf{v}} - \langle O_k\rangle_\rho\tag{14.8}\]

where \(O_k\) is the observable corresponding to \(\theta_k\), \(\rho_\mathbf{v}\) is the clamped state (visible units fixed to data), and \(\rho\) is the free state (thermal). Computing these requires approximating Gibbs states, which is hard classically but natural on quantum annealers (e.g. D-Wave).

Note

D-Wave quantum annealers can directly sample from the Gibbs distribution \(\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) of Eq. (14.6) for Ising-type Hamiltonians, making them natural hardware for QBM training.

docs.title: 14.4 Implementation: QGAN for Continuous Distributions
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

n_qubits = 4
n_layers = 2
dev_gen  = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits)
dev_disc = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits)

# -- Generator --------------------------------------------------
@qml.qnode(dev_gen, interface="torch", diff_method="parameter-shift")
def generator(weights):
    """PQC generator: maps |0> to target-like state distribution."""
    qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers(weights, wires=range(n_qubits))
    return [qml.probs(wires=i) for i in range(n_qubits)]

# -- Discriminator (classical neural net) ----------------------
class ClassicalDiscriminator(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim=n_qubits):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(in_dim, 16),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(16, 8),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(8, 1),
            nn.Sigmoid()
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x).squeeze(-1)

# -- Born machine (pure quantum generator) ---------------------
@qml.qnode(dev_gen, interface="torch", diff_method="parameter-shift")
def born_machine(weights):
    """Born machine: sample bitstrings from circuit distribution."""
    qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers(weights, wires=range(n_qubits))
    return qml.probs(wires=range(n_qubits))

# -- Training setup --------------------------------------------
gen_weights = torch.tensor(
    np.random.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi, (n_layers, n_qubits, 3)),
    dtype=torch.float32, requires_grad=True
)
disc = ClassicalDiscriminator()
opt_g = torch.optim.Adam([gen_weights], lr=0.05)
opt_d = torch.optim.Adam(disc.parameters(), lr=0.01)

# Target: bimodal distribution over 4-bit strings
# Real data: mix of strings near 0000 and 1111
def sample_real(batch=32):
    data = []
    for _ in range(batch):
        if np.random.rand() > 0.5:
            data.append([0.9, 0.1, 0.9, 0.1])  # near 0101
        else:
            data.append([0.1, 0.9, 0.1, 0.9])  # near 1010
    return torch.tensor(data, dtype=torch.float32)

def sample_generator(weights, batch=32):
    """Sample marginal probabilities from generator."""
    probs = generator(weights)  # list of 4 [p0, p1] tensors
    samples = torch.stack([p[:, 0] for p in probs], dim=-1)  # P(0) per qubit
    return samples.expand(batch, -1)

# -- Training loop ---------------------------------------------
losses_g, losses_d = [], []
for epoch in range(200):
    # - Discriminator update -
    real_data = sample_real(32)
    fake_data = sample_generator(gen_weights, 32).detach()
    opt_d.zero_grad()
    d_real = disc(real_data)
    d_fake = disc(fake_data)
    loss_d = -torch.mean(torch.log(d_real + 1e-8)
                         + torch.log(1 - d_fake + 1e-8))
    loss_d.backward()
    opt_d.step()

    # - Generator update -
    fake_data_g = sample_generator(gen_weights, 32)
    opt_g.zero_grad()
    d_fake_g = disc(fake_data_g)
    loss_g = -torch.mean(torch.log(d_fake_g + 1e-8))
    loss_g.backward()
    opt_g.step()

    losses_g.append(loss_g.item())
    losses_d.append(loss_d.item())

    if (epoch + 1)
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1:3d} | "
              f"Loss_G: {loss_g.item():.3f} | "
              f"Loss_D: {loss_d.item():.3f}")

# -- Born machine: train with MMD -----------------------------
bm_weights = torch.tensor(
    np.random.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi, (n_layers, n_qubits, 3)),
    dtype=torch.float32, requires_grad=True
)
opt_bm = torch.optim.Adam([bm_weights], lr=0.05)

# Target: uniform distribution over 4-bit strings
target_probs = torch.ones(2**n_qubits) / (2**n_qubits)

for epoch in range(150):
    opt_bm.zero_grad()
    gen_probs = born_machine(bm_weights)
    # KL divergence as MMD approximation
    mmd_loss = torch.sum(target_probs * torch.log(
        target_probs / (gen_probs + 1e-9) + 1e-9
    ))
    mmd_loss.backward()
    opt_bm.step()
    if (epoch + 1)
        tv = 0.5 * torch.sum(torch.abs(gen_probs - target_probs)).item()
        print(f"Born Machine Epoch {epoch+1} | "
              f"KL: {mmd_loss.item():.4f} | TV: {tv:.4f}")

print("\nFinal Born machine distribution (first 8 states):")
final_probs = born_machine(bm_weights).detach().numpy()
for i in range(8):
    print(f"  |{i:04b}> : {final_probs[i]:.4f}  "
          f"(target: {target_probs[i].item():.4f})")

docs.title: 14.5 Comparison: Classical vs. Quantum Generative Models
docs.text:
Table 14.1. Comparison of generative model approaches Model Distribution Training Sampling Expressibility Classical GAN Implicit Adversarial Fast High (neural) VAE Explicit ELBO Fast Medium Born Machine Born rule MMD/KL \(O(2^n)\) Quantum circuits QGAN Quantum Adversarial \(O(n)\) shots Quantum circuits QBM Gibbs Grad descent Thermal Hamiltonian

Research Highlight

Quantum supremacy for generation: Google’s 53-qubit Sycamore processor demonstrated sampling from a random circuit distribution that would take 10,000 years classically (Arute et al., 2019). While this is not a practical generative modelling task, it establishes that quantum circuits can produce distributions that are classically intractable, potentially offering a route to quantum advantage in generative modelling.

docs.title: 14.6 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • QGAN: Quantum generator (PQC) + quantum/classical discriminator. Training minimizes trace distance between real and generated quantum states.

  • Born machine: Circuit output probability \(p_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = |\langle\mathbf{x}|U(\boldsymbol{\theta})|0\rangle|^2\). Trained via MMD or KL divergence. Can represent classically hard distributions.

  • QBM: Gibbs state of a transverse-field Ising model. Natural hardware: quantum annealers. Gradient requires clamped and free Gibbs states.

  • Quantum advantage: RQC distributions are believed classically hard, but practical advantage for real-world generative tasks remains open.

Exercises

Exercise . Explain the Born rule and why it naturally defines a valid probability distribution over measurement outcomes. Why is this advantageous for generative modelling?

Exercise . Derive the gradient of the MMD loss in Eq. (14.5) with respect to a quantum circuit parameter \(\theta_k\) using the parameter-shift rule.

Exercise . Train a 4-qubit Born machine to reproduce a Gaussian distribution over 4-bit integers (e.g. centered at 8 with \(\sigma=2\)). Compare the learned distribution using total variation distance.

Further Reading

  • Lloyd & Weedbrook (2018) (Lloyd and Weedbrook 2018) — quantum GAN theory

  • Liu & Rebentrost (2018) (Liu and Wang 2018) — Born machines

  • Amin et al. (2018) (Amin et al. 2018) — Quantum Boltzmann machines

  • Arute et al. (2019) — Quantum supremacy using a programmable processor

docs.title: Chapter 15: Optimization and Training of Quantum Models
docs.text:
Training variational quantum circuits requires computing and applying gradients in a quantum-compatible way. This chapter presents the complete theory of the parameter-shift rule (PSR), quantum natural gradient (QNG), Rotosolve, SPSA, and advanced optimizers. We also discuss the challenges of gradient estimation noise, shot budgets, and practical training recipes for NISQ devices.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Derive the full parameter-shift rule for arbitrary generators

  • Implement quantum natural gradient with the quantum Fisher information metric

  • Apply Rotosolve for exact trigonometric function minimization

  • Estimate gradients under finite-shot noise and design shot budgets

  • Select appropriate optimizers for different quantum training scenarios

docs.title: 15.1.1 Single-Parameter Shift Rule
docs.text:
Consider a quantum circuit \(U(\theta) = e^{-i\theta G/2}\) where \(G\) is a Hermitian generator with eigenvalues \(\pm r\) (for \(r=1/2\), this is Pauli rotations).

Definition: Parameter-Shift Rule (Mitarai et al., 2018; Schuld et al., 2019)

For a circuit \(U(\theta) = e^{-i\theta G/2}\) with generator eigenvalues \(\pm r\), the gradient of expectation value \(f(\theta) = \langle\hat{O}\rangle_\theta\) is:

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta} = r\left[f\!\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{4r}\right) - f\!\left(\theta-\frac{\pi}{4r}\right)\right]\tag{15.1}\]

For Pauli rotations (\(G\in\{X,Y,Z\}\), \(r=1/2\), shift \(s=\pi/2\)):

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta} = \frac{1}{2}\left[f\!\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{2}\right) - f\!\left(\theta-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right]\tag{15.2}\]

Proof sketch: Since \(U(\theta)|\psi\rangle\) is periodic in \(\theta\) (period \(4\pi\) for Pauli rotations), \(f(\theta)\) is a trigonometric polynomial. By Fourier analysis, the gradient of a trigonometric polynomial with frequencies \(\{r\}\) is exactly given by the finite difference formula Eq. (15.1).

docs.title: 15.1.2 Generalized Parameter-Shift Rule
docs.text:
For a generator \(G\) with arbitrary eigenvalue spectrum \(\{r_k\}\), the generalized PSR (Wierichs et al. 2022) is:

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta} = \sum_k c_k\, f(\theta + s_k)\tag{15.3}\]

where the shifts \(\{s_k\}\) and coefficients \(\{c_k\}\) are determined by the eigenvalue differences \(\{r_j - r_k\}\). For a generator with \(N\) distinct eigenvalues, at most \(2(N-1)\) evaluations are needed.

Solved Example 15.1

Problem: Apply the PSR to compute \(\partial\langle Z\rangle/\partial\theta\) for the circuit \(R_z(\theta)|+\rangle\).

Solution: Initial state: \(|+\rangle = (|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\). After \(R_z(\theta) = e^{-i\theta Z/2}\): \(|\psi(\theta)\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(e^{-i\theta/2}|0\rangle + e^{i\theta/2}|1\rangle)\).

Expectation: \(f(\theta) = \langle Z\rangle = \frac{1}{2}(e^{-i\theta/2}\cdot 1 \cdot e^{i\theta/2} + e^{i\theta/2}\cdot(-1)\cdot e^{-i\theta/2}) = 0\).

Hmm, \(f(\theta)=0\) always, so \(\partial f/\partial\theta = 0\).

Let us try \(\langle X\rangle\) instead: \(f(\theta) = \langle X\rangle = \cos\theta\). By PSR: \(\frac{1}{2}[f(\theta+\pi/2) - f(\theta-\pi/2)] = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(\theta+\pi/2) - \cos(\theta-\pi/2)] = \frac{1}{2}[-\sin\theta + \sin\theta]\cdot 2 = -\sin\theta\).

Verify: \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\cos\theta = -\sin\theta\). ✓

docs.title: 15.1.3 Gradient Estimation Under Finite Shots
docs.text:
With \(M\) shots per circuit evaluation, the gradient estimator has variance:

\[\mathrm{Var}\left[\frac{\partial\hat{f}}{\partial\theta}\right] = \frac{1}{4M}\left[\mathrm{Var}[\hat{O}]_{\theta+s} + \mathrm{Var}[\hat{O}]_{\theta-s}\right] \leq \frac{1}{2M}\tag{15.4}\]

since \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat{O}]\leq 1\) for bounded observables \(\|\hat{O}\|\leq 1\).

Note

To achieve gradient estimation error \(\epsilon\), one needs \(M = O(1/\epsilon^2)\) shots per parameter per gradient step. For \(p\) parameters, total shots per step: \(2pM = O(p/\epsilon^2)\). This scales linearly in \(p\) – the same as classical automatic differentiation in terms of parameters, but with quantum overhead.

docs.title: 15.2 Quantum Natural Gradient
docs.text: Figure 15.1. Left: The parameter shift rule illustrated on a sinusoidal cost \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\). The exact gradient at \(\theta_0\) equals \([\mathcal{L}(\theta_0+s)-\mathcal{L}(\theta_0-s)]/2\) for any shift \(s\). Right: PSR provides exact gradients for all shift sizes, unlike finite differences whose error grows with \(s\). Figure drawn for this book

docs.title: 15.2.1 Motivation: Riemannian Optimization
docs.text:
Standard gradient descent on parameter space \(\mathbb{R}^p\) ignores the geometry of the quantum state space (a Riemannian manifold with the Fubini-Study metric). This leads to suboptimal trajectories and slow convergence.

Definition: Quantum Natural Gradient (Stokes et al., 2020)

The Quantum Natural Gradient (QNG) (Stokes et al. 2020) update is:

\[\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \eta\, F^{+}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\tag{15.5}\]

where \(F(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) is the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM):

\[F_{jk}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathrm{Re}\left[ \langle\partial_j\psi|\partial_k\psi\rangle - \langle\partial_j\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\partial_k\psi\rangle \right]\tag{15.6}\]

and \(F^+\) denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse.

The QNG moves along the steepest descent direction in the space of quantum states (Fubini-Study geometry), rather than Euclidean parameter space.

docs.title: 15.2.2 Computing the QFIM
docs.text:
Using the PSR, individual QFIM entries can be computed as:

\[F_{jk} = \frac{1}{2}\langle[G_j, G_k]\rangle + \frac{1}{4}\langle\{G_j, G_k\}\rangle - \langle G_j\rangle\langle G_k\rangle\tag{15.7}\]

For a \(p\)-parameter circuit, the QFIM has \(O(p^2)\) entries, each requiring \(O(1)\) circuit evaluations via Hadamard tests.

Tip

Block-diagonal approximation: In practice, use the block-diagonal approximation \(F \approx \text{blockdiag}(F_1, F_2, …)\) where each block corresponds to one layer. This reduces computation from \(O(p^2)\) to \(O(p)\) while preserving most of the geometric benefit.

docs.title: 15.3 Rotosolve
docs.text:
Definition: Rotosolve (Ostaszewski et al., 2021)

For a circuit \(U(\theta_k)\) where the \(k\)-th parameter appears only via \(R_y(\theta_k)\) (or any Pauli rotation), the loss \(f(\theta_k)\) is a trigonometric function:

\[f(\theta_k) = a\sin(\theta_k) + b\cos(\theta_k) + c\tag{15.8}\]

Rotosolve finds the exact global minimum in \(\theta_k\) using only 3 function evaluations:

\[\theta_k^* = -\frac{\pi}{2} - \arctan\left(\frac{2f(0) - f(\pi/2) - f(-\pi/2)}{f(\pi/2) - f(-\pi/2)}\right)\tag{15.9}\]

Rotosolve cycles through all parameters, updating each to its exact optimum while holding others fixed – a quantum coordinate descent.

Convergence: Rotosolve converges monotonically (loss decreases at each step). For \(p\) parameters, one full sweep requires \(3p\) circuit evaluations.

Solved Example 15.2

Problem: Apply one Rotosolve step to minimize \(f(\theta) = \sin\theta + 2\) starting from \(\theta_0 = 0\).

Solution: Evaluate at 3 points: \(f(0) = 0 + 2 = 2\), \(f(\pi/2) = 1 + 2 = 3\), \(f(-\pi/2) = -1 + 2 = 1\).

Apply formula: \(\theta^* = -\frac{\pi}{2} - \arctan\left(\frac{2(2) - 3 - 1}{3 - 1}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{2} - \arctan\left(\frac{0}{2}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{2}\).

Verify: \(f(-\pi/2) = -1 + 2 = 1 = \min_\theta[\sin\theta + 2]\). ✓

docs.title: 15.4 Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation
docs.text:
Definition: SPSA (Spall, 1992)

SPSA estimates the gradient using only 2 circuit evaluations regardless of the number of parameters:

\[\hat{\nabla}_\theta f \approx \frac{f(\boldsymbol{\theta}+c\Delta) - f(\boldsymbol{\theta}-c\Delta)}{2c}\,\Delta^{-1}\tag{15.10}\]

where \(\Delta\in\{-1,+1\}^p\) is a random Rademacher vector and \(c>0\) is a perturbation size. \(\Delta^{-1}\) denotes element-wise reciprocal.

SPSA convergence: Under standard conditions, SPSA achieves \(O(1/\sqrt{T})\) convergence in \(T\) iterations, same asymptotic rate as SGD but with \(O(1)\) circuit evaluations per step vs. \(O(p)\) for PSR.

Important

When to use each optimizer:

  • PSR + Adam: Default choice. Accurate gradients, GPU-friendly via PennyLane automatic differentiation.

  • QNG: When geometry matters (non-convex landscapes, small shot budgets). Higher per-step cost but faster convergence per iteration.

  • Rotosolve: For shallow circuits with independent single-qubit rotations. Guaranteed monotone descent, no learning rate tuning.

  • SPSA: Large \(p\) (many parameters), tight shot budgets, hardware experiments where circuit re-runs are expensive.

docs.title: 15.5.1 Optimal Shot Allocation
docs.text:
For \(p\) parameters each requiring gradient estimation, total shots per step:

\[M_{\text{total}} = 2p \cdot M_{\text{per-param}}\]

Frugal shot optimization: Allocate more shots to parameters with larger gradient magnitudes (importance sampling):

\[M_k \propto \left|\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\theta_k}\right| \quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_k M_k = M_{\text{total}}\]

docs.title: 15.5.2 Stochastic PSR
docs.text:
Use \(M=1\) shot per evaluation (stochastic gradient):

  • Much cheaper: \(2p\) circuit calls per step

  • Higher variance: requires more steps

  • Effective for large \(p\) regimes

docs.title: 15.6 Implementation: Optimizer Comparison
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml
import numpy as np
from pennylane import qchem

# Hydrogen molecule (minimal basis)
symbols  = ["H", "H"]
geometry = np.array([[0.0, 0.0, -0.6614], [0.0, 0.0, 0.6614]])

hamiltonian, n_qubits = qchem.molecular_hamiltonian(symbols, geometry)

dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits)
n_layers = 2

@qml.qnode(dev, interface="torch", diff_method="parameter-shift")
def ansatz(params):
    qml.BasisState(np.array([1, 1, 0, 0]), wires=range(n_qubits))
    qml.DoubleExcitation(params[0], wires=[0, 1, 2, 3])
    return qml.expval(hamiltonian)

import torch
import torch.optim as optim

def run_optimizer(opt_name, n_steps=200):
    params = torch.tensor([0.1], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
    if opt_name == "adam":
        opt = optim.Adam([params], lr=0.1)
    elif opt_name == "sgd":
        opt = optim.SGD([params], lr=0.05)

    losses = []
    for step in range(n_steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = ansatz(params)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
        losses.append(loss.item())
    return losses

# Run all optimizers
results = {}
for name in ["adam", "sgd"]:
    results[name] = run_optimizer(name)
    print(f"{name.upper():4s}: final E = {results[name][-1]:.6f} Ha")

# Quantum Natural Gradient (PennyLane built-in)
params_qng = np.array([0.1])
opt_qng = qml.QNGOptimizer(stepsize=0.1)

@qml.qnode(dev, diff_method="parameter-shift")
def ansatz_np(params):
    qml.BasisState(np.array([1, 1, 0, 0]), wires=range(n_qubits))
    qml.DoubleExcitation(params[0], wires=[0, 1, 2, 3])
    return qml.expval(hamiltonian)

qng_losses = []
for step in range(100):
    params_qng, loss_val = opt_qng.step_and_cost(ansatz_np, params_qng)
    qng_losses.append(loss_val)
    if (step + 1)
        print(f"QNG step {step+1:3d}: E = {loss_val:.6f} Ha")

# SPSA optimizer
params_spsa = np.array([0.1])
spsa_losses = []
c = 0.1  # perturbation
a = 0.05  # step size

for step in range(200):
    delta = np.random.choice([-1, 1], size=params_spsa.shape)
    f_plus  = ansatz_np(params_spsa + c * delta)
    f_minus = ansatz_np(params_spsa - c * delta)
    grad_est = (f_plus - f_minus) / (2 * c) * (1 / delta)
    # Decaying step size
    a_k = a / (1 + step * 0.01)
    params_spsa -= a_k * grad_est
    spsa_losses.append(ansatz_np(params_spsa))

print(f"\nSPSA final energy: {spsa_losses[-1]:.6f} Ha")
print(f"FCI reference:    -1.136189 Ha")

docs.title: 15.7 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • PSR: Exact quantum gradient via \(2p\) circuit evaluations. For Pauli generators: shift \(s=\pi/2\). Generalized to arbitrary generators with multiple frequencies (Wierichs et al., 2022).

  • QNG: Preconditions gradient with quantum Fisher information matrix (Fubini-Study metric). Faster convergence per iteration, higher per-step cost.

  • Rotosolve: Exact coordinate-wise minimization for single-parameter trigonometric functions. \(3p\) evaluations per sweep, monotone descent.

  • SPSA: 2 evaluations per step regardless of \(p\). Stochastic gradient, useful for hardware experiments.

  • Shot budgets: Allocate shots proportional to gradient magnitude for efficient optimization under hardware constraints.

Exercises

Exercise . Prove that the parameter-shift rule \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta} = \frac{1}{2}[f(\theta+\pi/2) - f(\theta-\pi/2)]\) gives the exact gradient when \(f(\theta) = a\cos\theta + b\sin\theta + c\).

Exercise . For a 6-parameter VQC, compare the total number of circuit evaluations per gradient step for: (a) PSR, (b) SPSA, (c) finite differences with \(\epsilon=0.01\). Which is most shot-efficient? Which is most accurate?

Exercise . Implement the Rotosolve optimizer from scratch (no PennyLane built-in) for a 4-parameter circuit. Compare convergence rate (loss vs. circuit evaluations) against Adam+PSR on a 1D problem (VQE for H2).

Further Reading

  • Mitarai et al. (2018) (Mitarai et al. 2018) — original parameter-shift rule

  • Schuld et al. (2019) (Schuld et al. 2019) — PSR for arbitrary generators

  • Stokes et al. (2020) (Stokes et al. 2020) — quantum natural gradient

  • Ostaszewski et al. (2021) — Rotosolve and Rotoselect

  • Wierichs et al. (2022) (Wierichs et al. 2022) — generalized PSR

docs.title: Chapter 16: Barren Plateaus and Trainability of Quantum Models
docs.text:
Barren plateaus are regions in the parameter landscape of variational quantum circuits where gradients vanish exponentially with system size, rendering training impractical. This chapter presents the rigorous theory of barren plateaus, their causes (global cost functions, random initialization, noise, entanglement), and practical mitigation strategies including local cost functions, layer-wise training, identity blocks, and correlation-aware initialization.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • State the barren plateau theorem and its proof sketch

  • Identify which ansatz and cost function choices lead to barren plateaus

  • Distinguish noise-induced from expressibility-induced barren plateaus

  • Apply mitigation strategies: local costs, LBFGS, layerwise training

  • Design trainable ansatze that avoid barren plateaus

docs.title: 16.1 The Barren Plateau Phenomenon
docs.text:
Definition: Barren Plateau (McClean et al., 2018)

A barren plateau (McClean et al. 2018) occurs when, for a parameterized quantum circuit \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) and cost function \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \langle\hat{O}\rangle\), the gradient variance vanishes exponentially with system size \(n\):

\[\mathrm{Var}_\theta\left[\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\theta_k}\right] = O(b^{-n}), \quad b > 1\tag{16.1}\]

This means both \(\mathbb{E}[\partial_k\mathcal{L}] = 0\) and \(\mathbb{E}[|\partial_k\mathcal{L}|] = O(b^{-n/2})\), requiring exponentially many shots to estimate the gradient.

The physical intuition: if \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) is a 2-design (approximates Haar-random unitaries), all output states concentrate near the maximally mixed state, making the cost function flat everywhere.

docs.title: 16.2 Barren Plateau Theorem
docs.text:
Definition: Barren Plateau Theorem (McClean et al., 2018)

Let \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) be a random quantum circuit forming a 2-design on \(n\) qubits, and \(\mathcal{L} = \langle\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})|\hat{O}|\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle\) where \(\hat{O}\) is a global operator (\(\hat{O}\neq I^{\otimes k}\otimes\hat{o}\) for \(k=O(n)\)). Then:

\[\mathrm{Var}_\theta\left[\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\theta_k}\right] \leq \frac{\|\hat{O}\|_F^2}{2^{2n}-1} = O\!\left(\frac{1}{4^n}\right)\tag{16.2}\]

The gradient variance decays at least as fast as \(4^{-n}\).

Proof sketch:

  1. Write \(\partial_k\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}[\mathcal{L}(\theta_k+\pi/2) - \mathcal{L}(\theta_k-\pi/2)]\) (PSR).

  2. Decompose \(U(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = V_R R_k(\theta_k) V_L\) where \(V_{R,L}\) are the remaining circuit parts.

  3. Under Haar measure on \(V_L\), \(\rho_L = V_L|0\rangle\langle 0|V_L^\dagger\) concentrates near \(I/2^n\).

  4. The variance integral over \(V_L\) involves the second moment of the Haar measure, yielding the \(4^{-n}\) bound via the formula \(\mathbb{E}_U[U A U^\dagger \otimes U B U^\dagger] = \frac{\mathrm{Tr}[A]\mathrm{Tr}[B]}{d^2-1}I\) for \(d=2^n\).

docs.title: 16.3.1 Global Cost Functions
docs.text:
Important

Global vs. local costs: A cost function is global if it involves correlations between all \(n\) qubits (e.g. \(\hat{O} = |\mathbf{0}\rangle\langle\mathbf{0}|^{\otimes n}\), the \(n\)-qubit projector). It is local if it decomposes as \(\hat{O} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i\hat{o}_i^{(k)}\) where each \(\hat{o}_i^{(k)}\) acts on \(O(1)\) qubits around qubit \(i\).

Local costs avoid barren plateaus: their variance decays at most polynomially.

docs.title: 16.3.2 Expressibility-Induced Barren Plateaus
docs.text:
Highly expressible ansatze (those forming approximate \(t\)-designs) suffer exponentially vanishing gradients. There is a fundamental tension:

\[\text{Expressibility} \nearrow \implies \text{Barren Plateaus} \nearrow\tag{16.3}\]

Consequence: Shallow, structured ansatze (hardware-efficient, problem-inspired) may be better for training despite having lower expressibility.

docs.title: 16.3.3 Noise-Induced Barren Plateaus
docs.text:
Wang et al. (2021) (Wang et al. 2021) showed that depolarizing noise induces barren plateaus even in shallow circuits:

For a circuit of depth \(L\) with depolarizing noise rate \(\lambda\) per gate, the gradient decays as:

\[\mathrm{Var}[\partial_k\mathcal{L}] \leq O((1-\lambda)^{2L})\tag{16.4}\]

This grows exponentially worse with depth \(L\), making deep noisy circuits untrainable regardless of initialization.

docs.title: 16.3.4 Entanglement-Induced Barren Plateaus
docs.text:
Marrero et al. (2021) showed that highly entangled states in the latent space of QNNs lead to barren plateaus. Specifically:

\[\mathrm{Var}[\partial_k\mathcal{L}] \leq C\cdot e^{-S_2(\rho_A)}\tag{16.5}\]

where \(S_2(\rho_A) = -\log\mathrm{Tr}[\rho_A^2]\) is the Rényi-2 entropy of a subsystem \(A\).

docs.title: 16.4 Mitigation Strategies
docs.text: Figure 16.1. Left: Gradient variance scaling with qubit count for global costs (\(\propto 2^{-n}\)), local costs (\(\propto 1/n^2\)), and noise-induced BPs (\(\propto e^{-\alpha n}\)). Right: A trainable 2-parameter loss landscape (small circuit) vs the flat barren plateau region for large circuits. Figure drawn for this book

docs.title: 16.4.1 Local Cost Functions
docs.text:
Replace global cost with local equivalents:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{local}} = 1 - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \langle Z_i\rangle \quad\text{vs.}\quad \mathcal{L}_{\text{global}} = 1 - \langle\mathbf{0}|^{\otimes n}\rho|\mathbf{0}\rangle^{\otimes n}\tag{16.6}\]

Cerezo et al. (2021) (Cerezo et al. 2021) proved that local costs have polynomial (rather than exponential) gradient decay with depth.

docs.title: 16.4.2 Identity Block Initialization
docs.text:
Initialize each parameterized block to the identity: \(U(\mathbf{0}) = I\). This keeps the circuit near identity at initialization, where gradients are \(O(1)\) before training (Grant et al., 2019).

Identity block construction:

At \(\theta_1=\theta_2=0\): circuit is identity (up to global phase). Small perturbations give \(O(1)\) gradients.

docs.title: 16.4.3 Layer-Wise Training
docs.text:
Train the circuit layer by layer:

  1. Fix all layers except layer 1 to identity; train layer 1 until convergence

  2. Fix layer 1; add and train layer 2

  3. Repeat until all \(L\) layers are trained

  4. Fine-tune all layers jointly

This prevents deep circuits from entering the barren plateau regime during early training.

docs.title: 16.4.4 Problem-Informed Ansatze
docs.text:
Use the symmetries and structure of the problem:

  • UCCSD ansatz: Chemically motivated, respects particle conservation

  • QAOA: Problem Hamiltonian structure guides circuit design

  • Equivariant circuits: Circuits that commute with symmetry operators of the problem; guaranteed to stay in relevant subspace

Solved Example 16.1

Problem: For a 10-qubit random circuit (2-design), estimate the gradient standard deviation \(\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\partial_k\mathcal{L}]}\) for (a) a global cost function and (b) a 1-local cost function.

Solution:

(a) Global cost: By the barren plateau theorem: \(\mathrm{Var}[\partial_k\mathcal{L}] \leq 4^{-10} = 4^{-10} \approx 10^{-6}\). Gradient std \(\approx 10^{-3}\). Detecting this requires \(\sim 10^6\) shots.

(b) 1-local cost: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{local}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i\langle Z_i\rangle\). Each term involves only a single-qubit observable. Using a local version of the barren plateau theorem, variance scales as \(O(1/4)\) (2-qubit subsystem, independent of \(n\)). Gradient std \(\approx 0.5\).

The local cost requires only \(O(1)\) shots to estimate the gradient, compared to \(O(4^n)\) for the global cost – an exponential improvement.

docs.title: 16.5 Diagnosing Barren Plateaus
docs.text:
Algorithm: Barren Plateau Diagnosis Protocol

  1. Gradient variance scaling: Plot \(\log\mathrm{Var}[\partial_k\mathcal{L}]\) vs. \(n\) (system size). Exponential decay \(\Rightarrow\) barren plateau.

  2. Loss landscape visualization: For 2 parameters, 2D loss surface. Flat surface \(\Rightarrow\) barren plateau.

  3. Training trajectory: Monitor gradient norms. Exponentially small norms stall training.

  4. Chebyshev bound check: \(P(|\mathcal{L} - \bar{\mathcal{L}}| \geq \epsilon) \leq \mathrm{Var}[\mathcal{L}]/\epsilon^2\). If variance is exponentially small, training is exponentially unlikely to escape.

docs.title: 16.6 Implementation: Barren Plateau Detection
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def get_gradient_variance(n_qubits, n_samples=200, use_local=False):
    """
    Estimate gradient variance for random circuit of size n_qubits.
    Returns Var[d_loss/d_theta] for a single parameter.
    """
    dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_qubits)
    n_layers = 3

    if use_local:
        # Local cost: average single-qubit Z
        @qml.qnode(dev, diff_method="parameter-shift")
        def circuit(params):
            qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers(params, wires=range(n_qubits))
            return [qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(i)) for i in range(n_qubits)]

        def cost(params):
            return -np.mean(circuit(params))
    else:
        # Global cost: fidelity with |00...0>
        @qml.qnode(dev, diff_method="parameter-shift")
        def circuit(params):
            qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers(params, wires=range(n_qubits))
            return qml.expval(
                qml.Hermitian(
                    np.diag([1] + [0]*(2**n_qubits - 1)),
                    wires=range(n_qubits)
                )
            )
        cost = circuit

    gradients = []
    for _ in range(n_samples):
        # Random initialization
        params = np.random.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi,
                                   (n_layers, n_qubits, 3))
        params = qml.numpy.array(params, requires_grad=True)
        grad = qml.grad(cost)(params)
        gradients.append(float(grad[0, 0, 0]))  # first parameter gradient

    return np.var(gradients)

# Scan qubit counts
qubit_counts = [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
vars_global = []
vars_local  = []

for n in qubit_counts:
    v_glob = get_gradient_variance(n, n_samples=100, use_local=False)
    v_loc  = get_gradient_variance(n, n_samples=100, use_local=True)
    vars_global.append(v_glob)
    vars_local.append(v_loc)
    print(f"n={n}: Var[global]={v_glob:.2e}, Var[local]={v_loc:.2e}")

# Identity block initialization vs random
print("\n--- Initialization Strategy Comparison ---")
n = 6
dev6 = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n)
n_layers = 3

@qml.qnode(dev6, diff_method="parameter-shift")
def local_circuit(params):
    qml.StronglyEntanglingLayers(params, wires=range(n))
    return [qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(i)) for i in range(n)]

def local_cost(params):
    return -np.mean(local_circuit(params))

# Random initialization
grads_random = []
for _ in range(50):
    p = qml.numpy.array(
        np.random.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi, (n_layers, n, 3)),
        requires_grad=True
    )
    g = qml.grad(local_cost)(p)
    grads_random.append(np.abs(g[0, 0, 0]))

# Near-zero initialization (identity block approximation)
grads_identity = []
for _ in range(50):
    p = qml.numpy.array(
        np.random.normal(0, 0.1, (n_layers, n, 3)),  # small params
        requires_grad=True
    )
    g = qml.grad(local_cost)(p)
    grads_identity.append(np.abs(g[0, 0, 0]))

print(f"Random init   mean |grad|: {np.mean(grads_random):.4f} "
      f"+/- {np.std(grads_random):.4f}")
print(f"Identity init mean |grad|: {np.mean(grads_identity):.4f} "
      f"+/- {np.std(grads_identity):.4f}")

docs.title: 16.7 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • Barren plateaus: Exponential vanishing of gradient variance \(\mathrm{Var}[\partial_k\mathcal{L}] = O(4^{-n})\) for global cost + random ansatz. Makes training exponentially costly.

  • Causes: Global cost functions, 2-design expressibility, depolarizing noise (noise-induced BP), high entanglement.

  • Local costs: Decompose observable as sum of \(O(1)\)-qubit terms. Variance scales polynomially, not exponentially.

  • Initialization: Identity blocks, near-zero initialization, structured (UCCSD/QAOA) ansatze all help avoid BPs.

  • Layerwise training: Add layers sequentially after convergence to prevent deep circuits from entering BP regime at initialization.

Exercises

Exercise . Explain in words why a random quantum circuit that forms a 2-design leads to barren plateaus. What property of 2-designs causes the gradient to vanish?

Exercise . Prove that for \(n=2\), the local cost function \(\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}(\langle Z_0\rangle + \langle Z_1\rangle)\) has gradient variance \(O(1/4)\) for a Haar-random 2-qubit unitary, while the global cost \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{global}} = \langle|00\rangle\langle00|\rangle\) has gradient variance \(O(1/16)\).

Exercise . Reproduce the barren plateau scaling plot: for \(n = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10\) qubits, estimate gradient variance for both global and local cost functions with 3-layer strongly entangling circuits. Verify the exponential vs. polynomial scaling.

Further Reading

  • McClean et al. (2018) (McClean et al. 2018) — original barren plateau paper

  • Cerezo et al. (2021) (Cerezo et al. 2021) — local cost functions mitigate BPs

  • Wang et al. (2021) (Wang et al. 2021) — noise-induced barren plateaus

  • Marrero et al. (2021) — entanglement-induced barren plateaus

  • Grant et al. (2019) — identity initialization strategy

docs.title: Chapter 17: NISQ Hardware Platforms
docs.text:
Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices are today’s quantum computers: 50–1000 qubits, limited coherence times, imperfect gates, restricted connectivity. This chapter surveys the four main hardware platforms — superconducting circuits, trapped ions, photonic systems, and neutral atoms — covering their physical principles, noise models, gate sets, and implications for QML algorithm design.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Describe the operating principles of each major NISQ hardware platform

  • Identify the native gate sets and connectivity graphs of IBM, IonQ, and Rigetti

  • Model hardware noise using depolarizing, dephasing, and amplitude damping channels

  • Transpile and optimize quantum circuits for specific hardware topologies

  • Select appropriate hardware based on QML task requirements

docs.title: 17.1.1 Physical Principles
docs.text:
Superconducting qubits are lithographically fabricated circuits (aluminum on silicon) cooled to \(\sim15\) mK. The qubit is formed by the transmon: a Josephson junction shunted by a large capacitor, creating an anharmonic quantum oscillator with non-degenerate energy levels.

\[H_{\text{transmon}} = 4E_C(\hat{n}-n_g)^2 - E_J\cos\hat{\phi}\tag{17.1}\]

where \(E_C\) is charging energy, \(E_J\) is Josephson energy, and \(n_g\) is the offset charge. The qubit is the two-level system \(\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}\) corresponding to the ground and first excited states.

Key parameters (typical IBM quantum):

  • Qubit frequency: \(4\)–\(6\) GHz

  • \(T_1\) (relaxation): \(50\)–\(500\) \(\mu\)s

  • \(T_2\) (dephasing): \(50\)–\(300\) \(\mu\)s

  • Single-qubit gate time: \(\sim50\) ns; error \(\sim0.05\%\)

  • Two-qubit (CNOT) gate time: \(\sim300\) ns; error \(\sim0.5\%\)–\(1\%\)

docs.title: 17.1.2 Native Gate Set and Connectivity
docs.text:
IBM Quantum uses:

  • Native 1Q gates: \(\{R_z(\theta), SX, X\}\)

  • Native 2Q gate: \(\text{ECR}\) or \(\text{CX}\) (CNOT)

  • Connectivity: Heavy-hex lattice (each qubit connected to 2–3 neighbors)

Note

The heavy-hex connectivity restricts CNOT availability. All-to-all connectivity would require SWAP gates (3 CNOTs each) for non-adjacent qubits, increasing circuit depth by \(O(\sqrt{n})\) for most algorithms.

docs.title: 17.2.1 Physical Principles
docs.text:
Trapped-ion quantum computers use individual atomic ions (e.g. \(^{171}\)Yb\(^+\), \(^{133}\)Ba\(^+\)) confined in electromagnetic (Paul) traps. The qubit is encoded in two electronic states (hyperfine or optical transitions).

Advantages over superconducting:

  • \(T_1 > 10\) minutes (vs. \(\mu\)s for superconducting)

  • All-to-all connectivity via collective motional modes

  • High fidelity: 1Q \(> 99.9\%\), 2Q \(> 99.5\%\)

  • Low crosstalk: ions are well-separated (\(\sim10\) \(\mu\)m)

Disadvantages:

  • Slower gates: 2Q gate \(\sim100\) \(\mu\)s (vs. 300 ns superconducting)

  • Scalability: trapped-ion chains limited to \(\sim50\) qubits (motional mode crowding)

docs.title: 17.2.2 Mølmer-Sørensen Gate
docs.text:
The native 2Q gate for trapped ions is the Mølmer-Sørensen (MS) gate:

\[MS(\chi) = \exp\!\left(-i\frac{\chi}{2}(X\otimes X)\right)\tag{17.2}\]

For \(\chi=\pi/2\): MS\((\pi/2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&-i\\0&1&-i&0\\0&-i&1&0\\-i&0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\), which can generate maximally entangled states.

docs.title: 17.3 Photonic Quantum Computing
docs.text:
Photonic quantum computers encode qubits in photon states (dual-rail encoding: \(|0\rangle\) = photon in lower path, \(|1\rangle\) = photon in upper path) or continuous-variable systems (coherent/squeezed states).

Continuous-variable (CV) QML (Xanadu Strawberry Fields):

  • Gates: displacement \(D(\alpha)\), squeezing \(S(r)\), beamsplitter \(BS(\theta,\phi)\)

  • Measurement: homodyne (Gaussian), photon number (non-Gaussian)

  • Advantage: room temperature operation, high speed (\(\sim\)MHz clock)

  • Disadvantage: non-Gaussian resources required for universal computation

Key CV gates:

\[\begin{align*} \text{Squeezing:}& \quad S(r) = e^{r(\hat{a}^2-\hat{a}^{\dagger 2})/2} \\ \text{Displacement:}& \quad D(\alpha) = e^{\alpha\hat{a}^\dagger - \alpha^*\hat{a}} \\ \text{Beamsplitter:}& \quad BS(\theta) = e^{\theta(\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{b}-\hat{a}\hat{b}^\dagger)} \end{align*}\]

docs.title: 17.4 Neutral Atom Arrays
docs.text:
Neutral atom processors (Rydberg arrays: Harvard, QuEra, Pasqal) trap neutral atoms in reconfigurable optical tweezer arrays. Qubits are encoded in hyperfine ground states.

Rydberg blockade mechanism: When two atoms are within blockade radius \(R_b\), the Rydberg interaction prevents simultaneous excitation:

\[V(r) = \frac{C_6}{r^6} \gg \Omega \quad\text{for}\quad r < R_b\tag{17.6}\]

This implements a controlled-\(Z\) (CZ) gate between neighboring atoms.

Advantages:

  • 2D connectivity: atoms arranged in arbitrary 2D geometry

  • Large system sizes: 256+ qubits demonstrated (Ebadi et al., 2021)

  • Reconfigurable: atoms can be moved between shots

  • Analog mode: directly simulate Ising Hamiltonians

docs.title: 17.5 Hardware Noise Models
docs.text: Figure 17.1. Left: Radar chart comparing four NISQ platforms (superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic, neutral-atom) across five performance dimensions (schematic). Right: Gate error rate trends from 2016–2024 for superconducting and trapped-ion platforms. Figure drawn for this book

docs.title: 17.5.1 Depolarizing Channel
docs.text:
\[\mathcal{E}_{\text{dep}}(\rho) = (1-p)\rho + \frac{p}{3}(X\rho X + Y\rho Y + Z\rho Z)\tag{17.7}\]

Shrinks the Bloch vector by factor \((1-4p/3)\). Models random Pauli errors.

docs.title: 17.5.2 Dephasing (Phase-Damping) Channel
docs.text:
\[\mathcal{E}_{\text{deph}}(\rho) = (1-p)\rho + p Z\rho Z\tag{17.8}\]

Destroys off-diagonal coherences: \(\rho_{01} \to (1-2p)\rho_{01}\).

docs.title: 17.5.3 Amplitude Damping Channel
docs.text:
Models energy relaxation (\(T_1\) decay):

\[\mathcal{E}_{\text{AD}}(\rho) = K_0\rho K_0^\dagger + K_1\rho K_1^\dagger\tag{17.9}\] \[K_0 = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\sqrt{1-\gamma}\end{pmatrix}, \quad K_1 = \begin{pmatrix}0&\sqrt{\gamma}\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\]

where \(\gamma = 1-e^{-t/T_1}\) is the decay probability.

docs.title: 17.5.4 Platform Comparison
docs.text: Table 17.1. NISQ platform comparison (approximate 2024 values) Platform Qubits \(T_1\) Gate Error (2Q) Connectivity Gate Speed Superconducting (IBM) 127+ \(100\,\mu\)s \(0.5\)–\(1\%\) Heavy-hex \(300\) ns Trapped ion (IonQ) 32+ \(> 1\) min \(< 0.5\%\) All-to-all \(100\,\mu\)s Photonic (Xanadu) 216 N/A \(\sim1\%\) Programmable \(\sim\)ns Neutral atom (QuEra) 256 \(> 1\) s \(0.5\)–\(1\%\) Reconfigurable \(\mu\)s

docs.title: 17.6 Circuit Transpilation
docs.text:
Transpilation converts a logical circuit to hardware-native form:

  1. Gate decomposition: Express all gates in native gate set

  2. SWAP routing: Insert SWAP gates for non-adjacent CNOTs

  3. Optimization: Cancel redundant gates, merge rotations

  4. Scheduling: Minimize circuit depth via parallelism

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
from qiskit_aer.noise import (NoiseModel, depolarizing_error,
                               amplitude_damping_error)
from qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider import FakeNairobi

# Build a simple VQC
qc = QuantumCircuit(4, 4)
qc.h(range(4))
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.cx(1, 2)
qc.cx(2, 3)
qc.ry(0.5, range(4))
qc.measure(range(4), range(4))

# Get real hardware noise model from IBM fake backend
backend = FakeNairobi()
noise_model = NoiseModel.from_backend(backend)

# Transpile to hardware native gate set
transpiled = transpile(qc, backend=backend, optimization_level=3)
print(f"Original depth:    {qc.depth()}")
print(f"Transpiled depth:  {transpiled.depth()}")
print(f"Original gates:    {qc.count_ops()}")
print(f"Transpiled gates:  {transpiled.count_ops()}")

# Simulate with noise
sim = AerSimulator()
sim.set_options(noise_model=noise_model)
job = sim.run(transpiled, shots=2048)
counts = job.result().get_counts()

# Compare noiseless vs noisy
sim_ideal = AerSimulator()
job_ideal = sim_ideal.run(transpile(qc, sim_ideal), shots=2048)
counts_ideal = job_ideal.result().get_counts()

# Total variation distance
from collections import defaultdict
all_keys = set(counts) | set(counts_ideal)
p_noisy = {k: counts.get(k, 0)/2048 for k in all_keys}
p_ideal = {k: counts_ideal.get(k, 0)/2048 for k in all_keys}
tv = 0.5 * sum(abs(p_noisy[k] - p_ideal[k]) for k in all_keys)
print(f"\nTotal variation distance (noisy vs ideal): {tv:.4f}")

# Custom noise model
custom_noise = NoiseModel()
# Depolarizing error after each CNOT
cnot_error = depolarizing_error(0.01, 2)  # 1
custom_noise.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(cnot_error, ['cx'])
# Amplitude damping for all 1Q gates (T1 ~ 50us, gate time 50ns)
gamma = 1 - np.exp(-50e-9 / 50e-6)  # P(decay) per 1Q gate
t1_error = amplitude_damping_error(gamma)
custom_noise.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(t1_error, ['u', 'rz', 'sx'])

print(f"\nAmplitude damping rate per gate: {gamma:.6f}")
print(f"This means T1 decay is {'negligible' if gamma < 1e-4 else 'significant'}")

docs.title: 17.7 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • Superconducting (IBM, Google, Rigetti): Fast gates (ns), nearest-neighbor connectivity, \(T_1\sim100\,\mu\)s. Dominant platform.

  • Trapped ion (IonQ, Quantinuum): Slow gates (\(\mu\)s), all-to-all connectivity, very high fidelity. Best for algorithms requiring many 2Q gates.

  • Photonic (Xanadu): Room temperature, high speed, CV framework, non-Gaussian operations needed for universality.

  • Neutral atoms (QuEra, Pasqal): Large scale (256+ qubits), reconfigurable 2D geometry, Rydberg blockade for 2Q gates.

  • Noise models: Depolarizing (random Pauli), dephasing (\(T_2\) decay), amplitude damping (\(T_1\) decay). Use Qiskit for hardware-accurate simulation.

Exercises

Exercise . Compare trapped-ion and superconducting qubits on four dimensions: gate speed, coherence time, connectivity, and scalability. For which QML tasks would you prefer each platform?

Exercise . Derive the Bloch vector evolution under a depolarizing channel with rate \(p\). Show that after \(L\) identical gates, the Bloch vector magnitude is \((1-4p/3)^L\).

Exercise . Using Qiskit’s FakeBackend, transpile a 5-qubit QAOA circuit with \(p=2\) layers and measure: (a) circuit depth before and after transpilation, (b) CNOT count, (c) approximate simulation accuracy using TVD between noisy and noiseless runs.

Further Reading

  • Krantz et al. (2019) — superconducting qubits review

  • Bruzewicz et al. (2019) — trapped-ion quantum computing

  • Arute et al. (2019) — Google quantum supremacy (superconducting)

  • Ebadi et al. (2021) — 256-atom Rydberg quantum simulator

  • Weedbrook et al. (2012) — Gaussian quantum information (photonics)

docs.title: Chapter 18: Quantum Error Mitigation
docs.text:
Quantum error correction (QEC) requires fault-tolerant hardware beyond current reach. Quantum error mitigation (QEM) is a family of classical post-processing techniques that suppress noise effects on near-term devices without physical ancillas. This chapter covers zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), Clifford data regression (CDR), readout error mitigation, and symmetry verification.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Distinguish quantum error correction from quantum error mitigation

  • Apply zero-noise extrapolation to recover noiseless expectation values

  • Implement probabilistic error cancellation using quasi-probability decompositions

  • Use Clifford data regression to train noise-aware surrogate models

  • Apply readout error mitigation and symmetry verification in Qiskit/Mitiq

docs.title: 18.1 Error Mitigation vs. Error Correction
docs.text:
Table 18.1. Quantum error correction vs. quantum error mitigation Property Error Correction (QEC) Error Mitigation (QEM) Overhead \(O(d^2)\) physical qubits per logical Classical post-processing Requires Fault-tolerant hardware NISQ devices Noise reduction Exponential (code distance \(d\)) \(O(1/\sqrt{M})\) in shots Scalable Yes (in principle) No (exponential sampling) Applications Fault-tolerant QC Near-term VQAs Cost Hardware (qubits) Classical (samples)

Definition: Quantum Error Mitigation

Quantum error mitigation techniques produce an estimate \(\tilde{E} = \langle\hat{O}\rangle_\text{ideal}\) of the noise-free expectation value from noisy circuit executions, at the cost of increased measurement overhead (more shots or more circuits).

docs.title: 18.2 Zero-Noise Extrapolation
docs.text:
Definition: Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE; Temme et al., 2017)

ZNE (Temme et al. 2017) runs circuits at multiple noise levels \(\{\lambda_1, \lambda_2, …, \lambda_k\}\) (\(\lambda_i > 1\) means amplified noise) and extrapolates to the zero-noise limit \(\lambda\to0\).

Noise amplification methods:

  1. Gate folding: Replace each gate \(G\) with \(GG^\dagger G\) (3\(\times\) noise amplification). For factor \(\lambda\): apply \(G(G^\dagger G)^{(\lambda-1)/2}\).

  2. Pulse stretching: Slow down microwave pulses on superconducting hardware (requires pulse-level access).

  3. Identity insertion: Insert pairs of canceling gates \(G G^\dagger\) at noise-sensitive locations.

Extrapolation models:

\[\begin{align*} E(\lambda) &= a + b\lambda & \text{(linear)} \\ E(\lambda) &= a + b\lambda + c\lambda^2 & \text{(quadratic)} \\ E(\lambda) &= ae^{-b\lambda} & \text{(exponential)} \end{align*}\]

At \(\lambda=0\): \(\tilde{E} = E(0) = a\) is the mitigated estimate.

Solved Example 18.1

Problem: A noisy circuit gives \(E(1) = 0.7\), \(E(2) = 0.5\), \(E(3) = 0.35\) (at noise factors 1, 2, 3). Use linear and quadratic extrapolation to estimate \(E(0)\).

Solution:

Linear (using only \(\lambda=1,2\)): \(E(\lambda) = a + b\lambda\). \(0.7 = a + b\), \(0.5 = a + 2b \Rightarrow b = -0.2\), \(a = 0.9\). \(\tilde{E}_\text{lin} = E(0) = 0.9\).

Quadratic (using \(\lambda=1,2,3\)): \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&2&4\\1&3&9\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\\c\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0.7\\0.5\\0.35\end{pmatrix}\)

Solving: \(a = 0.95\), \(b = -0.275\), \(c = 0.025\). \(\tilde{E}_\text{quad} = E(0) = 0.95\).

The quadratic model uses all data points and typically gives a better estimate when noise has a quadratic component.

docs.title: 18.2.1 Richardson Extrapolation
docs.text:
For polynomial noise models \(E(\lambda) = \sum_{k=0}^m a_k\lambda^k\), Richardson extrapolation at \(m+1\) noise levels gives exact recovery if the polynomial order is \(\leq m\):

\[\tilde{E} = \sum_{i=0}^m \gamma_i E(\lambda_i), \quad \gamma_i = \prod_{j\neq i}\frac{-\lambda_j}{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}\tag{18.4}\]

docs.title: 18.3 Probabilistic Error Cancellation
docs.text:
Figure 18.1. Left: ZNE – measured expectation values at noise scale factors \(\lambda=1,1.5,2,2.5,3\) are fit by a polynomial and extrapolated to \(\lambda=0\). Right: Mitigation error and sampling overhead comparison for ZNE (linear and quadratic), PEC, and CDR. Figure drawn for this book

Definition: Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC; Temme et al., 2017)

PEC (Temme et al. 2017) expresses the ideal circuit as a linear combination of implementable (noisy) circuits using quasi-probability decompositions:

\[\mathcal{E}_\text{ideal} = \sum_i c_i \mathcal{E}_i, \quad c_i\in\mathbb{R}\tag{18.5}\]

where \(\{\mathcal{E}_i\}\) are physically implementable (noisy) operations and \(\{c_i\}\) are real coefficients (can be negative — quasi-probabilities).

PEC estimator:

\[\tilde{E} = \gamma\sum_i \mathrm{sgn}(c_i) E_i\tag{18.6}\]

where \(\gamma = \sum_i|c_i|\) is the sampling overhead (one-norm of the quasi-probability).

Sampling overhead: To achieve estimator variance \(\leq\epsilon^2\), one needs \(M = O(\gamma^2/\epsilon^2)\) samples. For a circuit of \(L\) noisy gates each with quasi-probability \(\gamma_i\):

\[\gamma_\text{total} = \prod_{i=1}^L \gamma_i\tag{18.7}\]

This grows exponentially in circuit depth — PEC is exact but costly.

Note

For a single depolarizing gate with error rate \(p\), the quasi-probability one-norm is \(\gamma = 1 + 2p\), giving \(\gamma^2 - 1 \approx 4p\) overhead in sampling. For 100 gates at 1% error: \(\gamma_\text{total} = 1.02^{100} \approx 7.2\), requiring \(\approx 52\times\) more samples than noiseless.

docs.title: 18.4 Clifford Data Regression
docs.text:
Definition: Clifford Data Regression (CDR; Czarnik et al., 2021)

CDR (Czarnik et al. 2021) trains a classical regression model to predict the noise-free expectation value from noisy observations, using Clifford circuits (efficiently simulable classically) as training data.

CDR procedure:

  1. Generate near-Clifford circuits \(\{C_i\}\) by replacing most non-Clifford gates in the target circuit with nearest Clifford approximations.

  2. Simulate \(\{C_i\}\) classically to get \(\{E_i^\text{ideal}\}\) (exact).

  3. Execute \(\{C_i\}\) on hardware to get \(\{E_i^\text{noisy}\}\).

  4. Train regression model: \(E^\text{ideal} = a\cdot E^\text{noisy} + b\).

  5. Apply learned correction to target circuit’s noisy output: \(\tilde{E} = a\cdot E^\text{noisy}_\text{target} + b\).

CDR is effective when the noise model is similar across near-Clifford and target circuits.

docs.title: 18.5 Readout Error Mitigation
docs.text:
Readout errors (\(|0\rangle\to|1\rangle\) with probability \(p_{0\to1}\), \(|1\rangle\to|0\rangle\) with probability \(p_{1\to0}\)) are modeled by a calibration matrix \(A\):

\[\mathbf{p}_\text{noisy} = A\,\mathbf{p}_\text{ideal}\tag{18.8}\]

Measurement error mitigation: Invert \(A\) to recover \(\mathbf{p}_\text{ideal} = A^{-1}\mathbf{p}_\text{noisy}\).

Calibration: prepare all \(2^n\) computational basis states, measure the noisy probabilities to build \(A\). For large \(n\), use tensor-product approximation \(A \approx \bigotimes_i A_i\) (independent readout errors).

docs.title: 18.6 Symmetry Verification
docs.text:
For circuits that respect a symmetry \(S\) (e.g. particle number in chemistry), noisy outputs can be post-selected or reweighted using symmetry violations as an error indicator.

\[\tilde{E} = \frac{\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\mathcal{E}(\rho)} \cdot \mathrm{Tr}[S\,\mathcal{E}(\rho)]}{\mathrm{Tr}[S\,\mathcal{E}(\rho)]^2}\tag{18.9}\]

States with wrong symmetry eigenvalue are discarded (post-selection) or down-weighted (probabilistic).

docs.title: 18.7 Implementation with Mitiq
docs.text:
import mitiq
from mitiq import zne, pec, cdr
from mitiq.interface.qiskit import from_qiskit, to_qiskit
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
from qiskit_aer.noise import NoiseModel, depolarizing_error
import numpy as np

# -- Setup: noisy backend -------------------------------------
noise_model = NoiseModel()
noise_model.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(
    depolarizing_error(0.02, 1), ['u', 'rx', 'ry', 'rz']
)
noise_model.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(
    depolarizing_error(0.05, 2), ['cx']
)
sim = AerSimulator(noise_model=noise_model)

# -- Target circuit: GHZ state ---------------------------------
def make_ghz(n=4):
    qc = QuantumCircuit(n)
    qc.h(0)
    for i in range(n-1):
        qc.cx(i, i+1)
    return qc

qc = make_ghz(4)

# -- Executor function for Mitiq -------------------------------
def noisy_executor(circuit):
    """Run a Mitiq circuit on the noisy simulator, return <Z0>."""
    from qiskit import transpile
    qiskit_circuit = to_qiskit(circuit)
    qiskit_circuit.measure_all()
    transpiled = transpile(qiskit_circuit, sim)
    job = sim.run(transpiled, shots=8192)
    counts = job.result().get_counts()
    # Estimate <Z0>: +1 if bit 0 is 0, -1 if bit 0 is 1
    total = sum(counts.values())
    z0 = sum((-1)**int(bits[-1]) * count
             for bits, count in counts.items()) / total
    return z0

# Convert to Mitiq circuit
mitiq_circuit = from_qiskit(qc)

# -- Ideal result (noiseless) ---------------------------------
sim_ideal = AerSimulator()
def ideal_executor(circuit):
    from qiskit import transpile
    qc2 = to_qiskit(circuit)
    qc2.measure_all()
    job = sim_ideal.run(transpile(qc2, sim_ideal), shots=8192)
    counts = job.result().get_counts()
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return sum((-1)**int(b[-1]) * c for b, c in counts.items()) / total

ideal_value = ideal_executor(mitiq_circuit)
noisy_value = noisy_executor(mitiq_circuit)
print(f"Ideal <Z0>:       {ideal_value:.4f}")
print(f"Noisy <Z0>:       {noisy_value:.4f}")
print(f"Error:            {abs(ideal_value - noisy_value):.4f}")

# -- Zero-Noise Extrapolation ---------------------------------
# Scale noise by 1x, 2x, 3x using gate folding
zne_result = zne.execute_with_zne(
    mitiq_circuit,
    executor=noisy_executor,
    factory=zne.RichardsonFactory(scale_factors=[1, 2, 3])
)
print(f"\nZNE-mitigated <Z0>: {zne_result:.4f}")
print(f"ZNE error:          {abs(ideal_value - zne_result):.4f}")

# -- Exponential extrapolation --------------------------------
zne_exp = zne.execute_with_zne(
    mitiq_circuit,
    executor=noisy_executor,
    factory=zne.ExpFactory(scale_factors=[1, 2, 3], asymptote=0.0)
)
print(f"ZNE (exp) <Z0>:     {zne_exp:.4f}")

# -- Readout error mitigation ---------------------------------
from qiskit.utils.mitigation import complete_meas_cal, CompleteMeasFitter
from qiskit import transpile

n_qubits = 4
meas_calibs, state_labels = complete_meas_cal(
    qubit_list=range(n_qubits),
    qr=None, cr=None, circlabel='cal'
)
cal_jobs = sim.run(transpile(meas_calibs, sim), shots=8192)
cal_results = cal_jobs.result()
meas_fitter = CompleteMeasFitter(cal_results, state_labels)

print(f"\nReadout error mitigation matrix condition number: "
      f"{np.linalg.cond(meas_fitter.cal_matrix):.2f}")

docs.title: 18.8 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • ZNE: Run circuits at amplified noise levels, extrapolate to zero noise. Methods: gate folding, Richardson extrapolation, exponential fit. Cost: \(O(m)\) circuits for \(m\) noise levels.

  • PEC: Quasi-probability decomposition of ideal as linear combo of noisy operations. Exact but exponential sampling overhead \(\gamma^{2L}\).

  • CDR: Train regression on near-Clifford circuits (classically simulable). Effective for smooth noise models.

  • Readout mitigation: Calibration matrix \(A\); invert to correct measurement errors. Tensor-product approximation for large \(n\).

  • Symmetry verification: Post-select on correct symmetry sector. Free mitigation when problem has known symmetries.

Exercises

Exercise . Explain why ZNE works for polynomial (but not exponential) noise models at low noise levels. What is the systematic error of ZNE when the true noise model is exponential but linear extrapolation is used?

Exercise . A 10-gate circuit has depolarizing error rate \(p=0.02\) per gate. Calculate the PEC sampling overhead \(\gamma^2\) for the full circuit. How many times more shots does PEC require vs. raw noisy execution?

Exercise . Implement ZNE from scratch (no Mitiq) for a 4-qubit QAOA circuit: amplify noise by factors 1, 2, 3 using gate folding, fit a quadratic polynomial, and extract the \(\lambda=0\) value. Compare with Mitiq’s built-in ZNE.

Further Reading

  • Temme et al. (2017) (Temme et al. 2017) — ZNE and PEC original paper

  • Czarnik et al. (2021) (Czarnik et al. 2021) — Clifford data regression

  • Cai et al. (2023) — comprehensive quantum error mitigation review

  • LaRose et al. (2022) — Mitiq: an open-source package for error mitigation

docs.title: Chapter 19: QML for Quantum Chemistry and Molecular Simulation
docs.text:
Quantum chemistry is the most mature application domain for quantum computing. The electronic structure problem — finding ground-state energies of molecules — is QMA-hard classically but solvable efficiently on a quantum computer. This chapter covers the second-quantized Hamiltonian, VQE for molecular energy surfaces, quantum machine learning potentials (QMLPs), and property prediction for drug discovery.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Construct a second-quantized molecular Hamiltonian using the Jordan-Wigner transform

  • Implement VQE with UCCSD ansatz for H\(_2\) and LiH

  • Train a QML model to predict molecular potential energy surfaces

  • Apply quantum kernels to molecular fingerprint classification

  • Discuss the quantum advantage landscape for molecular simulation

docs.title: 19.1 The Electronic Structure Problem
docs.text:
The electronic Schrödinger equation for a molecule with \(N_e\) electrons and \(N_n\) nuclei (in atomic units):

\[\hat{H}\Psi(\mathbf{r}_1,…,\mathbf{r}_{N_e}) = E\Psi\tag{19.1}\] \[\hat{H} = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_i\nabla_i^2 - \sum_{i,A}\frac{Z_A}{|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{R}_A|} + \sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j|}\tag{19.2}\]

(Born-Oppenheimer approximation: nuclei fixed at \(\mathbf{R}_A\).)

Complexity: Classical methods:

  • Hartree-Fock: \(O(N_e^4)\) – mean-field, no correlation

  • MP2: \(O(N_e^5)\) – perturbative correlation

  • CCSD(T): \(O(N_e^7)\) – “gold standard,” limited to \(\sim50\) electrons

  • Full CI: \(O(\exp(N_e))\) – exact, intractable

A quantum computer with \(O(N_e)\) qubits can simulate the Hamiltonian efficiently via phase estimation or VQE.

docs.title: 19.2 Second Quantization and Qubit Mappings
docs.text:
In second quantization, the molecular Hamiltonian is:

\[\hat{H} = \sum_{pq} h_{pq}\hat{a}_p^\dagger\hat{a}_q + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{pqrs} g_{pqrs}\hat{a}_p^\dagger\hat{a}_q^\dagger\hat{a}_r\hat{a}_s\tag{19.3}\]

where \(\hat{a}_p^\dagger\), \(\hat{a}_p\) are fermionic creation/annihilation operators, \(h_{pq}\) are one-electron integrals, and \(g_{pqrs}\) are two-electron integrals.

docs.title: 19.2.1 Jordan-Wigner Transform
docs.text:
Maps fermionic operators to Pauli operators:

\[\begin{align*} \hat{a}_p^\dagger &= \left(\prod_{k<p}Z_k\right)\otimes\frac{X_p - iY_p}{2} \\ \hat{a}_p &= \left(\prod_{k<p}Z_k\right)\otimes\frac{X_p + iY_p}{2} \end{align*}\]

Result: The molecular Hamiltonian becomes a sum of Pauli strings:

\[\hat{H}_{\text{qubit}} = \sum_\alpha h_\alpha P_\alpha\tag{19.6}\]

where \(P_\alpha\in\{I,X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n}\) are \(n\)-qubit Pauli strings.

Solved Example 19.1

Problem: Write the Jordan-Wigner form of the number operator \(\hat{n}_0 = \hat{a}_0^\dagger\hat{a}_0\) for orbital \(p=0\).

Solution: \(\hat{n}_0 = \hat{a}_0^\dagger\hat{a}_0 = \frac{X_0-iY_0}{2}\cdot\frac{X_0+iY_0}{2} = \frac{X_0^2 + iX_0Y_0 - iY_0X_0 + Y_0^2}{4}\).

Using \(X^2=Y^2=I\) and \(XY=-YX=iZ\): \(= \frac{2I + 2Z}{4} = \frac{I+Z}{2} = |0\rangle\langle0|\).

This makes sense: \(\hat{n}_0\) measures whether orbital 0 is occupied (\(|0\rangle\) in JW convention means unoccupied, \(|1\rangle\) means occupied). Wait — JW convention: \(|0\rangle\) = unoccupied, \(|1\rangle\) = occupied. So \(\hat{n}_0 = \frac{I-Z}{2} = |1\rangle\langle1|\). ✓

docs.title: 19.3.1 UCCSD Ansatz
docs.text:
The Unitary Coupled Cluster Singles and Doubles (UCCSD) ansatz:

\[|\psi_{\text{UCCSD}}\rangle = e^{T-T^\dagger}|\text{HF}\rangle\tag{19.7}\]

where \(T = T_1 + T_2\) are the single and double excitation operators:

\[\begin{align*} T_1 &= \sum_{ia} t_i^a\hat{a}_a^\dagger\hat{a}_i \\ T_2 &= \sum_{ijab} t_{ij}^{ab}\hat{a}_a^\dagger\hat{a}_b^\dagger\hat{a}_j\hat{a}_i \end{align*}\]

Here \(i,j\) are occupied and \(a,b\) are virtual orbitals. The UCCSD ansatz is chemically motivated and hardware-implementable as a sequence of Givens rotations.

docs.title: 19.4 Quantum ML Potentials
docs.text:
Figure 19.1. Left: H\(_2\) potential energy surface computed by FCI (exact), VQE with UCCSD ansatz, and Hartree–Fock. VQE tracks FCI to within chemical accuracy (\(\leq 1.6\times 10^{-3}\) Ha). Right: VQE energy convergence at \(R=0.74\) Å. Figure drawn for this book

Quantum Machine Learning Potentials (QMLPs) learn molecular potential energy surfaces (PES) from quantum-computed reference data.

Architecture:

  1. Descriptor: Convert molecular geometry \(\{Z_i, \mathbf{r}_i\}\) to a rotationally/translationally invariant feature vector (e.g. Coulomb matrix, ACSF, SOAP descriptors)

  2. QML model: QNN or quantum kernel trained on descriptor \(\to\) energy

  3. Prediction: Predict energy \(E(\mathbf{r})\) and forces \(\mathbf{F}_i = -\nabla_{\mathbf{r}_i}E\)

Coulomb matrix descriptor for \(N\) atoms:

\[C_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0.5Z_i^{2.4} & i=j \\ \frac{Z_iZ_j}{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}_j|} & i\neq j \end{cases}\tag{19.10}\]

docs.title: 19.5 Quantum Kernels for Molecular Property Prediction
docs.text:
Molecular fingerprints (Morgan fingerprints, MACCS keys) can be used as inputs to quantum kernel methods for drug property prediction:

\[k_Q(m_1, m_2) = |\langle\phi(m_1)|\phi(m_2)\rangle|^2\tag{19.11}\]

where \(|\phi(m)\rangle = U_\phi(\text{fingerprint}(m))|0\rangle^n\).

Applications:

  • ADMET prediction: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity

  • Binding affinity: protein-ligand docking score prediction

  • Solubility: aqueous solubility from molecular structure

docs.title: 19.6 Implementation: VQE for H₂ and Molecular ML
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml
from pennylane import qchem
import numpy as np
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# -- Part 1: VQE for H2 at equilibrium geometry ---------------
symbols = ["H", "H"]
d_eq = 1.4  # Angstrom (equilibrium bond length)

def h2_hamiltonian(bond_length):
    """Build H2 Hamiltonian at given bond length."""
    geometry = np.array([[0.0, 0.0, -bond_length/2],
                          [0.0, 0.0,  bond_length/2]])
    H, n_qubits = qchem.molecular_hamiltonian(
        symbols, geometry,
        basis="sto-3g",
        method="rhf"
    )
    return H, n_qubits

H_eq, n_q = h2_hamiltonian(d_eq)
print(f"H2 Hamiltonian: {n_q} qubits, {len(H_eq.ops)} Pauli terms")

dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=n_q)

@qml.qnode(dev, diff_method="parameter-shift")
def vqe_circuit(params):
    """UCCSD-inspired ansatz for H2."""
    # Hartree-Fock reference state: |1100> (2 electrons in 4 spin-orbitals)
    qml.BasisState(np.array([1, 1, 0, 0]), wires=range(n_q))
    # Single excitation: orbital 0->2, 1->3
    qml.SingleExcitation(params[0], wires=[0, 2])
    qml.SingleExcitation(params[1], wires=[1, 3])
    # Double excitation: 01->23
    qml.DoubleExcitation(params[2], wires=[0, 1, 2, 3])
    return qml.expval(H_eq)

# Optimize
params = np.array([0.1, 0.1, 0.1], requires_grad=True)
opt = qml.GradientDescentOptimizer(stepsize=0.4)
energies = []
for step in range(150):
    params, energy = opt.step_and_cost(vqe_circuit, params)
    energies.append(energy)
    if (step + 1)
